#### The Organizing Society: 

##### GDMB Society for Mining, Metallurgy, Resource and Environmental Technology 

The GDMB is a non-profit organization. Its activities focus on combining science with practical experience in the fields of mining, engineering, tunnelling, mineral processing, extraction, recycling and refining of metals, as well as on the manufacturing of semi and finished products. There is an increasing emphasis on associated environmental issues. The GDMB is internationally active with a European basis and covers a wide variety of topics from applied geology via processing to recycling. These include many important areas of chemistry, especially the complex metallurgical chemistry and, last not least, also analytical chemistry. As a consequence of their increasing importance, aspects of industrial minerals are addressed in addition to the traditional fields of metals and alloys. In order to remain a vibrant and attractive professional society, the GDMB draws on the experience and interests of its worldwide members.

#### Preface 

###### Copper – Indicator of the progress of civilization 

This is the motto for the 7<sup>th</sup> international copper conference, the most important copper seminar in the world, which has been organized by the GDMB, the German based Society for Mining, Metallurgy, Resource and Environmental Technology, together with IIMCh from Chile, MetSoc from Canada, TMS, SME from USA and MMIJ from Japan. 

The copper conferences bring together the highest level of science and technology: universities, metal producers, manufacturing companies, suppliers and finally the people who work with copper: scientists, technicians, engineers, traders and many more. 

An extensive programme has been arranged for this conference and an abundance of contributions from all over the world dealing with the different aspects of copper making and its use are registered already, for which we gratefully thank the authors. Apart from plenary addresses, separate sessions will be held for economics, mineral processing, pyrometallurgy, hydrometallurgy, electrowinning and -refining, downstream fabrication and application, process control and automation, recycling and sustainable development, environmental control, health and safety. Copper, one of the oldest metals used by mankind, is still today one of the most important industrial metals and indispensable for modern life. It is the indicator of industrialization and progress in every country. It is used everywhere, where electricity flows and thus is still valued so highly today. The increased economic potential of newly industrialized countries, above all East Asia and China, has increased the significance of the red metal once again. More recent technologies in production, processing and application often provide new answers to old questions. From the middle of the last century there was another innovation surge resulting in totally new technologies, a trend still going on. This has made each copper conference into an exciting adventure. It is positive and reassuring that particularly the high industrialized countries have become the vanguard, not just in technical innovation, but also protection of environment and nature and preserving resources. They repeatedly prove that ecology and economy may go hand in hand. 

Many sponsors have contributed to the conference’s success, for which I would like to express my sincere thanks! 

Hamburg is expecting its guests! Hamburg, the old Hanseatic city with a 1200 year long tradition, o

ne of the biggest and most beautiful cities in Germany, combines a wonderful mixture of industry, commerce, nature and culture. Not only the “Copper 2010” in the Congress Centre awaits you, but rich offerings of sightseeing and shopping in a cosmopolitan city, one of the largest harbours in Europe, the Alster lake in the city centre, green parks and plenty of cultural events, some of which we hope to show you in the companions programme. 

We are delighted that you will join us and look forward to a highly interesting conference! 

_Michael Kopke_ Chairman Copper 2010

###### Is the Copper Industry Fit for the Future? 

Dr.-Ing. Bernd Drouven, CEO, Aurubis AG, Hamburg, Germany 

The copper world has already changed a great deal during recent years. But what still lies ahead of us? What are the changes in conditions that we have to cope with and how will our solutions look? 

The rise in the demand for raw materials is unrelenting. At the same time, both the primary and secondary feed materials have a specific complexity, the customers’ needs are becoming increasingly differentiated and their orders are placed at increasingly short notice. Production times for metals have to be faster and inventories minimised. 

The volatility of the metal prices has increased significantly in recent years and we will probably have to live with that in the future as well. The LME functioned well in the crisis, but the copper price is being influenced more and more by funds. 

How can the value added chain change to adapt to this? Which consequences will that have for process technology, production planning and logistics? How will the consolidation of our industry continue? 

This keynote will go into the various effects and challenges – in particular from the perspective of a European custom smelter and fabricator – and present possible approaches for solutions. 

###### Sustainable Growth Strategy for Japanese Copper Business 

Toshinori Kato, Managing Director, Mitsubishi Materials Corporation, Tokyo, Japan 

Business environment, for any industry, has changed dramatically over the last decade. Copper industry is no exception and those involved are experiencing an unprecedented pe

riod of upheaval. The landscape of the market has completely altered, with large-scale M&As taking place among miners - creating an oligopoly situation - and a rapid expansion of smelting capacity within developing countries, driven by strong economic growth. Traditional copper smelters and fabricators have been facing challenges, but a long-term sustainability of Japanese copper business is achievable. 

Firstly, an immense amount of effort has been made over the years to develop the clean and one of the most environmentally-friendly processes in the industry. Mitsubishi Materials (MMC) particularly plays a great role in establishing Japanese smelters’ reputation as the most energy-efficient operations in the world. It is our strong commitment to be a leader in this expertise by sharing our technologies with the industry. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

IX 



Secondly, infrastructures for copper smelting have been utilized in developing the recycling business. Exemplified by the operations at Onahama smelter, which has the world’s largest furnace for treatment of shredder residue, the industry has worked closely with other sectors and municipalities. Building an effective structure to make the best use of our facilities is a key for success in this field. It is fair to say that Japanese copper smelters, including MMC, are now regarded as an indispensable part of national environmental policy. 

Finally, progression of integration in the copper fabrication sector has strengthened the industry’s capability of providing a variety of high-value-added products to end-users. Tight relationships with the consumers have been beneficial in developing new use of copper. Evidence of a promising future can be seen in increasing use of copper in the growing sectors such as hybrid automobiles and renewable energy. 

###### Copper Sulphide Smelting: Past Achievements and Current Challenges 

Dr. Carlos M. Dнaz, Adjunct Professor, University of Toronto, Private Consultant, Toronto, Canada 

In the last three decades, increased oxygen consumption in copper sulphide smelting and converting and the implementation of computerized process control, among other factors, have led to higher process intensity and smelter concentrate processing capacity, decreased smelting energy consumption and improved SO2 capture from process gas streams. An annual primary smelting furnace throughput of one million tonnes of concentrate is the new industry standard. Top submerged lance smelting has become an important processing route in recent years. Two new continuous converting routes were commercialized in the 1990s. However, due to substantially improved converting practice and larger converters, Peirce-Smith converting still maintains its position as the dominant technology. 

A major realignment of world copper smelting has taken place in the last 30 years. Spurred by rapid economic expansion and the resulting huge increase in demand for basic materials, a number of modern, la

rge capacity copper smelters have been built in China, India and other Asian countries. Only moderate growth in smelting and electrorefining capacity has taken place elsewhere. Moreover, ER cathode output in the USA has substantially decreased. 

In this paper, the author examines recent technological advances and industry changes and highlights issues, such as energy consumption and the corresponding greenhouse gas emissions that will become the focus of future discussion. 

###### Energy as a Key Factor of Sustainability 

Javier Targhetta, Vice President, Freeport McMoRan, Phoenix, Arizona, USA 

Energy must be seen as the prime mover for development and is therefore vital for economic equilibrium and social welfare. Energy will continue to play a key role in the coming decades being not only an environmental challenge but also a fundamental issue in terms of the progress of humanity. Nevertheless, harmonizing several aspects related to energy management will be of essence for the 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

X 



near future and will make energy one of the greatest challenges of the 21<sup>st</sup> century. It is becoming increasingly important to maintain the appropriate equilibrium between environmental issues (global warming, the future of nuclear waste, the integration of renewable energies…), coordinated governments policies to ensure that global energy costs are kept competitive and companies finding a balanced, rational and fair model of energy utilization based on the review of ethical business aspects and the establishment of social responsibility principles. 

This paper develops the idea that the rules and procedures for future energy use must be based on a reasonable equilibrium between technical aspects mainly associated to environmental issues, political decisions made by governments and public administrations and social responsibility programmes that companies themselves must assume and implement. 

###### <mark>The Supply and Copper Producer Response to a Growing Demand Scenario</mark> 

Ricardo Alvarez, General Manager, Codelco El Teniente Division, Santiago, Chile 

<mark>The prospects for medium and long-term consumption of copper are promising. A recovery projected for developed economies, starting 2010, joins the growing impact on demand generated from the process of development and urbanization of emerging countries. The intensity of copper use will also maintain the positive growth started a decade ago based on factors such as providing solutions to combat global warming.</mark> 

<mark>The objective of this presentation is to analyze how supply may react and adjust to envisaged demand scenarios, bearing in mind some distinctive elements of the copper industry like:</mark> 

- <mark>Historical supply reaction to demand and price levels</mark> 

- <mark>Availability of resources and copper ore reserves, incorporating a dynamic analysis and the effects of geological exploration and possible technological changes.</ma

rk> - Pipeline of probable and possible projects, analysing the effects of projects in less developed and riskier geographical locations - Technological changes under development that may positively impact the amount of reserves available and the competitiveness of projects. - The growing role of scrap as a supply source for copper. Yun Zeng, Dr. Richard Woodling|| _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ XVII # Downstream Fabrication, Application and New Products _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 1 _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 2 ### Spray-formed Copper Alloys Have Become Mature Igor Altenberger, Hilmar Mьller, Robert Zauter Wieland-Werke AG Graf-Arco-StraЯe 36 Ulm, Germany **Keywords:** Spray forming, tin bronzes, multicomponent, bronzes, CuMn20Ni20, ITER #### Abstract Spray forming, also called spray casting, is a primary shaping method between continuous casting and powder metallurgy. It generates highly alloyed material which cannot be cast or further hot- and cold worked if produced by casting. Spray forming creates homogeneous microstructures in terms of grain size, phase and element distribution. This process enables highly alloyed materials to be producible and offered to the industry as a semi-finished product. More than 15 years have passed, since spray-formed copper alloys were introduced to the market the first time. The early years were characterized by progressive research and developments. The process of constant improvements is continuing while spray-formed copper alloys have become mature. The alloys are established in several special applications, e.g. steel working tools, metal injection plungers, supercond

uctor wire and components in oil drilling tools. These applications have one common feature: They are all associated with a bunch of ambitious requirements to the material which can only be fulfilled by highly alloyed copper material with isotropic properties of the spray formed-billets. 

Established alloys are aluminium bronzes with 12 % or more aluminium, tin bronzes with 14 % or more tin, a high-strength non-magnetic alloy with 20 % manganese and 20 % nickel as well as a highly conductive high-strength alloy with 7 % nickel and 2 % silicon. The process of spray forming guarantees a suitable microstructure which is necessary for both, the producibility of semi-finished products and the high performance properties during field application. In the shape of rods and tubes the material has to fulfill the customer designed combination of property requirements, e.g. nonmagnetism plus high strength plus high ductility in case of oil drilling tools, high compressive strength plus no galling tendency to steel plus good machinability in case of steel forming tools. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

3 

_Altenberger, Mьller, Zauter_ 



#### 1 Introduction 

Spray forming is a sophisticated material processing method for producing round-shaped billets, tubes or sheets which are further processed into semi-finished products [1]. Spray forming has successfully been applied in commercial production of steel [2, 3], aluminium alloys [4] and high strength copper alloys [5-11]. Other applications are Ni-base-super-alloys or refractory metals [12]. 



Figure 1: Role of Copper and Copper Alloys as advanced superconductors in ITER (picture by Kozo Osamura, Department of Materials Science and Engineering, Kyoto University, IWCC Technical Seminar, Tokyo (Nov. 2005)). Basic initial materials for Nb3Sn superconductive cables are copper-tin-bronzes and niobium rods. 

Wieland-Werke AG spray forms high alloyed aluminium bronzes for the tool and mould construction industry [13], a high-performance CuMnNi-alloy for oil-drilling equipment as well as high-tin bronzes for superconducting wire [5, 9, 10, 11]. Spray-formed copper alloys have been established in several cutting-edge technologies of the 21<sup>st</sup> century such as the International Thermo-nuclear Experimental reactor ITER in Cadarache, France, where they have been considered as lowtemperature superconductor cables (Figure 1). Other applications already in service are hot- and cold-working tools and equipment for the oil-drilling offshore/onshore industry, where either high strength at elevated temperature plus good thermal conductivity or a combination of high strength, low magnetic permeability and good corrosion resistance are essential, respectively. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

4 

_Spray-formed Copper Alloys Have Become Mature_ 



Figure 2 exhibits the spray forming facility at Wieland-Werke AG, basically using the Osprey process for billet production. In this facility, a single free-fall atomizer

is used with a typical deposition rate of 30 kg/min. Rotation-symmetrical billets with a typical diameter between 160 mm and 500 mm and a length of 2.2 m are produced. For detailed archival literature about this facility see [9]. Spray forming has been widely recognized as an elegant manufacturing method for generating microstructures or material states which by other conventional manufacturing methods, such as continuous casting, are not easily or not at all producible due to problems in segregations or castability, especially in alloy systems with broad solidifying intervals [1]. Today, spray forming is able to produce homogeneous billets of large geometry with fairly low porosity, especially after surface region removal by machining. Hot and cold porosity, which are inevitable in spray-formed materials, can be controlled by the gas/metal flow rate and by reactive elements, e.g. titanium [6, 7]. By careful selection of process parameters porosity can be kept to a minimum. Porosity levels of 1 % or lower can be achieved in the centre of the billet for mass production. In addition, a subsequent non-destructive inspection by an ultrasonic probe detects remaining critical porosity and thus maintains quality assurance. Smaller porosities are mostly eliminated during the subsequent hot-extrusion process. 1 Holding Furnace

Figure 2: Spray forming facility at Wieland-Werke AG. 5 _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ _Altenberger, Mьller, Zauter_ A broad variety of copper alloys have been produced by spray forming in the past two decades (e.g. CuCrZr-, CuNiSn-alloys or oxide dispersion strengthened copper alloys) [8], however this report will be confined to spray-formed high-tin bronzes (such as CuSn14.5Ti0.25), Cu-Ni-Mn-alloys, ternary high alloyed aluminium bronze (e.g. CuAl13.2Fe4.5Mn1Co1) and CuNi7Si2Cr. #### 2 High Strength Copper-Nickel-Manganese alloy Spray-formed CuMn20Ni20 is a high strength, non-magnetic alloy and offers an interesting combination of properties for materials used in oil drilling equipment. It is used as a construction material for rods in offshore/onshore oil drilling exploration and has comparable mechanical properties to high strength steel, titanium alloys or beryllium-copper [5, 11]. Since it is non-magnetic, it can be used for rods containing sensors and electronics for orientation purposes. CuMn20Ni20 (WielandLV7) is an age-hardenable alloy, therefore appropriate heat treatment can tailor the desired mechanical properties. Figure 3 illustrates the mechanical properties of spray-formed and extruded Cu20Mn20Ni in different aging conditions. Although stainless steels and beryllium-copper exhibit comparable or higher ductility and comparable tensile strength, respectively, CuMn20Ni20 offers a bette

r combination of strength and ductility. The basic strengthening mechanism in this alloy is precipitation hardening by ordered tetragonal MnNi-precipitates [14] serving as dislocation obstacles and thus improving the tensile- and yield strength. The heat treatment comprises a solution treatment followed by artificial aging. Spray formed and extruded CuMn20Ni20 offers a good corrosion resistance and resistance against stress corrosion cracking, thermal long term stability and good impact energy of > 20 J. Moreover, it can be cold worked easily and machined in the soft (solution heat treated), medium hard (partially aged) and hard condition. Tensile strength varies from 500 to 1400 MPa, depending on the aging condition of the material.

#### 3 Aluminium Bronzes 

Spray-formed aluminium bronzes contain 13-15 % aluminium and some percentage of other elements, e.g. Fe, Co. Accordingly, the microstructure contains a multitude of strength-giving phases (especially κ- and γ2-phases) leading to high hardness, compressive strength and high temperature strength [13]. Their strength, hardness and wear resistance are superior to conventionally cast aluminium bronzes. Additionally, they exhibit excellent corrosion resistance, machinability and a low galling tendency to steel. Due to the existence of the high temperature β-Phase, various thermomechanical treatments can be applied to aluminium bronzes. Appropriate isothermal tempering or controlled cooling rate can tailor the phase composition of the aluminium bronze. Generally, the hightemperature phase, named β-phase, is transformed into α- and γ2-phase below 565 °C by eutectoid decomposition. However, this eutectoid reaction is usually suppressed during cooling with industrial cooling rates, and instead, the martensite β'-phase is formed. The more γ2 is formed, the higher the wear resistance and brittleness and the lower the corrosion resistance of the alloy. The room temperature- and high temperature strength of aluminium bronzes up to 300 °C is usually obtained by finely distributed precipitates. In addition to γ2- and β'-, various iron-rich κ-precipitates are formed between 800 °C and 900 °C increasing strength and improving corrosion resistance. Typical applications of spray-formed aluminium bronzes are hot- and cold working tools (Figure 4) for steel production, profiling tools, deep drawing tools and tools in die-casting machines. Spray-formed aluminium bronzes are isotropic high performance materials helping to save production cost by low wear, longer tool life cycle time, less machine down times and lower cost for spare tools.

Here, spray-formed CuNi7Si2Cr is an excellent alternative, combining high strength and good ductility. Spray-formed CuNi7Si2Cr is an age-hardenable copper alloy which can be hot-extruded or forged into rods, tubes or more complex shapes. In this alloy, similar to Corson-alloys [17], precipitation hardening gives rise to Ni- and Cr-silicides, leading to excellent strength at ambient as well as at elevated temperatures. Figure 5 shows the yield strength of spray-formed, hot extruded and peak-aged CuNi7Si2Cr as well as other copper materials, stainless austenitic steel and aluminium alloys as a function of temperature. It can be seen, that the yield strength at elevated temperatures is superior to austenitic stainless steel and conventional high performance copper alloys up to 700 °C (The very expensive Ni- and Co-base alloys, titanium aluminides and refractory metals are not considered in this comparison). Hence, spray-formed and hot-extruded CuNi7Si2Cr is an excellent material for high-temperature applications, e.g. for die-casting plungers. #### 5 High-tin bronze for low temperature superconductors For high magnetic field strengths usually low-temperature superconductors of the Nb3Sn-type are used. Nb3Sn-superconducting wire, consisting of up to 10,000 Nb3Sn -filaments and the bronze matrix are produced from high-tin bronzes typically containing 13.5-16 % tin. The so-called "bronze route" for the Nb3Sn-wire production consists of several hot co-extrusion processes of Nb and bronze, drawing and diffusion heat treatment (Figure 6.). High-tin bronzes are chosen for an assembly of sheath tubes and hexagon tunes, or alternatively, for gun-drilled billets. Absolutely crucial is a high critical current density in Nb3Sn. Therefore the requirements for the homogeneity of the bronze are quite challenging: Good hot and cold workability for drawing thin wires is an absolute must. Especially the risk of constriction or fracture of the niobium filaments during wire drawing must be minimized by a suitable homogeneous precipitation structure of the bronze. A low level of segregations and a fine grain structure in high-tin bronzes can be achieved by spray forming. Figure 6 shows the microstructure of a spray-formed high-tin bronze from Wieland-Werke AG as produced by the Osprey process for spray forming of billets, using a free fall atomizer, and for comparison, the same alloys as produced by conventional casting. In certain applications they have become competitors to classical engineering materials such as steels or nickel alloys due to their homogeneous and tailored microstructure allowing production of complex alloy systems with a good combination of strength, ductility, workability and physical properties. ### Influence of Electrolytic Copper Impurities on the Results of Copper Rod Plasticity Examination by AR Test 

A. Chmielarz, W. Baranek, G. Krawiec, D. Kopyto 

Instytut Metali Nieżelaznych Sowińskiego 5 44-100 Gliwice, Poland 

**Keywords:** Electrolytic copper, impurities in cathode copper, copper rod plasticity examination by AR test 

#### Abstract 

Currently the usefulness of electrolytic copper for manufacturing of specific products in copper processing plants is most often controlled by various tests used for determination of its physicochemical properties. From among the well known and used methods for testing of copper rod, which is produced from the cathodes manufactured in KGHM Polska Miedź S.A., copper plasticity test, so called AR test, is becoming more and more important. 

In the presented study, based on statistical analysis of the results of determination of composition of copper cathodes and produced copper rod as well as on AR test results, influence of individual impurities in cathode copper on its usefulness in plastic working was determined. The analysis provided grounds for determination of relations, in a form of regression equations, between the content of individual impurities and AR test results and for arranging the copper cathodes components in the order reflecting their increasing influence on copper rod plasticity. Additionally, also results of studies into technological conditions and parameters of copper electrorefining in KGHM are presented. 

#### 1 Introduction 

The requirements of copper cathodes consumers force the producers to meet the new and stricter standards of quality and purity of the cathodes and to guarantee properties of the produced copper rod, which is a semi-product in production of electric wires. 

The traditional methods for examination of the copper rod manufactured in KGHM Polska Miedź S.A. beside chemical analysis for determination of impurities content, cover also such physical parameters as: Spiral Elongation Test (SET, mm), mechanical strength Rm [MPa], electrical

conductivity [MS/m]. The relation between purity of electrolytic copper and some of the properties of the manufactured products has been known for a long time already and has its physical explanation. The relat

ionship between the content of impurities and electric conductivity was a subject of many studies [1-4]. It was demonstrated that copper electric conductivity decreases with the increase of their concentration. The degree of the decrease depends also on the type of impurities and their distribution in the metal crystalline structure. The order of the impurities according to the decreasing influence on the electric conductivity is as follows: P, Fe, Co, Si, As, Sb, Sn, Ni, Pb, Zn, Ag [4]. There are also other opinions presented in the literature regarding the influence of individual impurities on the electrolytic copper electric conductivity. 

Extensive studies were also conducted to determine relationship between temperature of copper softening, as measured by Spiral Elongation Test [5], and the type and amount of impurities [6-8]. With respect to the increase of copper softening temperature the results of some of the studies show the most harmful influence of the following impurities: Se, Te, Bi, S, Sb, As. Neutral or relatively neutral in view of copper softening temperature are: Fe, Ni, Co, Ag, while influence of Pb content is ambiguous. Like in the case of the relation between electric conductivity and content of individual impurities, also in the discussed influence of copper purity on SET test results the presented in literature opinions are not consistent. 

So called AR test, modelled after the method used in French company SCCC, was introduced into the routine copper rod quality control at KGHM in 2004. The AR test replaces or supplements currently used and more troublesome methods for copper rod examination and is one of the basic criteria for assessment of the quality of the product manufactured in KGHM. 

##### 1.1 What is AR test 

AR test, used in examination of copper rod produced in KGHM, is based on the following operations: 

1. Drawing of a test section of the rod through one drawing die from Ш = 8 mm to Ш = 6.3 mm. 

2. Holding of the test section of Ш = 6.3 mm at the temperature of 260 ± 2 °C for 10 minutes.<sup>_1)_</sup> 

3. Breaking of the samples with tensile testing machine using 250 mm test sample. 

The test result is calculated as a ratio of test sample elongation at the moment of sample destruction to the measured length of the test sample and is expressed in percents. 

AR test is conducted on individual production batches with frequency of every 8 coils. Usually one AR measurement is performed on a single coil. In the quality assessment of the manufactured copper rod both results of AR test and their stability are important. The AR test is not as widely described in literature as other methods for examination of electrolytic copper properties. Up till now it is not included in the Polish standards.

**Keywords:** Copper nanoparticles, Ultrasonic Spray Pyrolysis (USP), hydrogen reduction 

#### Abstract 

Copper nanoparticles were prepared from aqueous solution of copper (II) nitrate (Cu(NO)3.3H2O) by ultrasonic spray pyrolysis (USP) method. The particle size is controlled by varying the synthesis parameters of the USP method such as reaction temperature, precursor concentration, gas flow rate, type of reactive/carrier gas and frequen

cy of the atomizer. We intend to investigate the effect of furnace temperature and solution concentration on particle size and morphology under 1.3 MHz ultrasonic frequency and 1.0 l/min H2 gas flow rate conditions. Particles were characterized by X- ray diffraction (XRD), Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) and Energy Dispersive Spectrometry (EDS). The XRD pattern indicates fcc crystal structured copper and the calculated crystalline size using Scherrer Equation was about 49 nm. Spherical copper nanoparticles were monitored in SEM images with a diameter range of 36 ± 8.5 nm. It was observed that the obtained particle size increases with elevated temperature and reduction of the particle size depends on the decrease in concentration of solution. 

#### 1 Introduction 

Nanoparticles have been drawing more attention due to their unique properties such as electronic, optical, thermal, magnetic properties arising form particle dimension and high surface-to-volume ratio [1-4]. Besides the size dependency, chemical and physical features of the nanoparticles are also affected from the shape of the particles. Therefore, attempts have focused to produce the nanoparticles with desired size and shape morphology to obtain intended properties [5, 6]. 

Among diverse nanoparticles, ultra fine metallic copper powders have attracted substantial attention because they are a base for developing technology and industry [7-9]. The main reason of fascination for the copper nanoparticles is their excellent catalytic, optic, mechanic, electronic and

magnetic properties. These nanoparticles have a good potential for widespread application in electronic devices, catalytic process and also they can be used as additives in lubricants, polymers, coatings and inks [6-12]. Especially, the combination of lower electrical resistance, higher allowed current density and relatively low cost of the nanosized copper particles provides some advantages over noble metals such as gold and silver to be an alternative material for application in printed circuit boards and flexible electronics [13, 14]. In addition to electrical properties, copper nanoparticles create considerable interest as catalyzer as well as gold, silver and other traditional catalysts[2, 15]. Moreover, copper nanoparticles can be used in biotechnology as cancer cell killer and germicides [1]. 

A number of physical, chemical or mechanical based processes to fabricate copper nanoparticles with different size and shape morphology have been developed such as thermal decomposition, microwave heating, radiation methods, microemulsion, reverse micelles, laser ablation, polyol method, solvothermal method, reduction of copper salts, vapor decomposition, etc. [2-16]. However, pure metallic copper particles usually cannot be synthesized by the reduction of simple copper salts like copper chloride or copper sulfate in aqueous solution [17]. Among various productio

n techniques, ultrasonic spray pyrolysis (USP) is a versatile method to synthesize ultrafine particles in a wide range of composition, size and morphology from aqueous solution of metal salts. Metallic, intermetallic and also ceramic nanosized particles can be fabricated easily by USP method. Particle production in USP method is based on reduction or thermal decomposition of aerosol droplets generated from aqueous solution of metal salts by an ultrasonic atomizer [18-21]. Stopic and coworkers [22] synthesized nanosized copper powders by USP using copper sulfate and copper acetate at a temperature range between 800 and 1000 °C. They obtained copper nanoparticles from copper sulfate low concentration solution and also fabricated particles in submicron range when copper acetate was used as precursor. In this research, spherical copper nanoparticles with an average particle size of 36 ± 8.5 nm were produced by USP method using copper (II) nitrate salt at low temperature under hydrogen flow. Effects of reaction temperature and concentration of precursor solution on particle size and morphological characteristics of the powders were investigated. #### 2 Experimental Copper (II) nitrate salt (Cu(NO3)2.3H2O) and ethanol used in experiments were of analytical grade and were used as received without further purification. #### 4 Conclusion 

Copper nanoparticles were successfully fabricated by USP method using aqueous solution of copper (II) nitrate at reaction temperatures between 400 and 800 °C under hydrogen atmosphere. Cu particles obtained using 0.05 M precursor solutions at 400 °C, 600 °C and 800 °C have 36 ± 8.5 nm, 50 ± 16.3 nm and 218 ± 91.5 nm average particle sizes, respectively. Agglomeration and sintering of the nanoparticles becomes more active with elevated temperatures, and thus spherical nanocrystalline submicron particles were formed by aggregation of nanoparticles. In addition

to that, increasing of the copper (II) nitrate concentration in the aqueous solution also accelerates the sintering of the nanoparticles due to reducing of the distance between nucleated particles during reaction. Therefore, nanocrystalline copper particles in submicron range were fabricated using 0.2 M solution at 600 °C and their crystalline size was determined as 49 nm.

Besides, the ternary eutectic point is of special interest for industry because the presence of the P rich phase Cu3P, occurring at the ternary eutectic point, could influence the brittleness of the final bronze product. However, the presence of the ternary eutectic point and its position in the phase diagram are still questionable. Therefore, the basic aim of the presented experimental investigation is to describe and verify the known ternary system. The performed thermodynamic investigatio

n includes numerical simulations of the binary systems CuSn and CuP and the ternary system Cu-Sn-P in the Cu rich corner and an experimental investigation containing differential thermal analysis and annealing experiments for the binary and ternary systems. In addition, the identification of the phases and phase regions is based on SEM and light microscope investigations. 

#### 1 Introduction 

According to European standards the Sn-content in bronze is limited to 9 wt. % Sn in wrought alloys and to 13 wt. % in cast alloys. In the as-cast state, the microstructure of bronze consists of α- phase (α) and the eutectoid of the α- and δ-phase (δ). The large solidification interval is one of the reasons for the strong macrosegregation often observed in bronze castings. In addition, diffusion of Sn in the solid is rather small, which is the reason that one cannot use heat treatment to get rid of already formed segregations. The δ-phase, forming due to solid-solid transformation during cooling, is rather rigid but present as interdendritic precipitate which leads to inhomogeneities in the solidified material.

Most of the fundamental research related to bronze has been performed many years ago [1-9]. During the last decades the improvement of experimental methods, and with that of measurement accuracy, was remarkable. However, only little experimental work has been performed on the thermodynamics of the system Cu-Sn-P, thought to represent the thermo-dynamic behaviour of common technical bronze alloys. Already published phase diagrams and assessment work for the binary systems Cu-Sn and Cu-P [10-17] are based on experimental observations of the 1930’s to the 1980’s. Therefore, it makes sense to validate those results with present measurement methods. 

The ternary system itself was assessed by [13] by taking major publications on the binary and one experimental study on the ternary system [18] into account. Figure 1 shows two isopleths at 5 wt. % P to compare (a) the experimental work [18] and (b) the calculated values based on the assessment work of [13]. Based on the binary phase diagrams γ is included in the numerical assessment although it was not observed in the experimental study of Takemoto [18]. The circle marks in both plots the region close to the ternary eutectic point which is still under discussion [10]. The existence of a ternary eutectic point at CuSn14.8P4.5 mass % was proposed in several publications from 1910 to 1937 [19-22]. Other authors (e.g. [7, 23]) suggested that this “ternary eutectic” should rather be a transition reaction L+α→β+Cu3P. This was also concluded in the experimental study of Takemoto et al. [18] (Figure 1a).

In the isothermal section at _T_ = 780 °C, β is present as a result of the peritectic reaction L + α → β starting at _T_ = 799 °C. With solidification of the third phase, the three phase region α-β-L (Figure 3, _T_ = 780 °C) can be observed. In the isothermal section at _T_ = 700 °C, γ is occurring as a result of the peritectic reaction L + β → γ at _T_ = 756 °C, and the three phase region β-γ-L appears. Besides, the eutectic groove between α and Cu3P is reached and the three phase region α-Cu3P-L is visible (Figure 3, _T_ = 700 °C). Further cooling leads to a decrease of the L region to a small area at _T_ = 648 °C. At slightly lower temperature, namely at approximately _T_ = 644 °C, the ternary eutectic point is reached at a concentration of 15 wt. % Sn and 5.5 wt. % P (number _T_ E, Figure 4a). 





Figure 4: (a) 3D liquidus surface of the Cu rich corner of Cu-Sn-P is displayed up to 35 wt. % Sn and 14 wt. % P. (b) Calculated isopleth for the same P concentration as displayed in Figure 1. Calculated with Thermo-Calc (database CuSnII). 

At _T_ = 648 °C the decrease of the liquid phase leads to the presence of two more three phase regions, namely Cu3P-γ-L and Cu3P-ε-γ. The ε-phase (ε) is located at ~38 wt. % Sn in the binary phase diagram and therefore its one phase region (appearing as a point in the isothermal section) is not visible in the presented ternary sections. In the isothermal section at _T_ = 640 °C the ξ-phase (ξ) occurs in the three phase region Cu3P-γ-ξ as a result of the peritectoid reaction ε + γ → ξ. Since ξ has a Sn content of approximately 36 wt.% Sn the one phase region of the binary system is also not visible in the ternary sections. 

The liquid phase has already disappeared at _T_ = 640 °C and four three phase regions are present, namely Cu3P-ε-ξ, Cu3P-γ-ξ, Cu3P-β-γ, and Cu3P-α-β. At _T_ = 525 °C the δ−phase (δ) has already appeared while ξ disappeared as a result of the peritectoid reaction ξ + γ → δ. In this section the three phase regions of Cu3P-δ-ε, and Cu3P-α-δ are present. With further cooling only the solubility of Sn in α is decreasing and therefore at _T_ = 400 °C the same phases are stable as at _T_ = 525 °C. Further decrease in temperature leads to the eutectoid reaction δ → α + ε at _T ~_ 350 °C and therefore δ is not present in the isothermal section at _T_ = 300 °C. At this temperature the phase regions of Cu3P, α and ε are connected by the three phase region Cu3P-ε-α.

(1) β (bright gray), (2) transformation area, (3) α (dark gray). #### 5 Conclusions The presented study includes a comparison of the numerical description of the ternary phase diagram Cu-Sn-P in the Cu rich corner based on calculations using database CuSnII and Thermo-Calc, annealing and diffusion experiments. The phase detection is based on microscopy and SEM investigations. The experimental observations show good agreement with the proposed ternary phase diagram of [13]. The detection of γ in the ternary sample CuSn30P1 and in the two samples of CuSn20P6 after 61 _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ _Grasser, Ludwig, Riedle, Schillinger_ annealing at 640 °C and 642 °C is in good agreement with the thermodynamic calculations but controversy to the absence of γ in the DTA measurements of [18]. Here further investigations are ongoing for more information about the conditions of the appearance of the γ-phase. In addition, ε was detected in binary samples with high Sn contents as proposed by thermodynamic data of Massalsky [11] or Miettinen [13]. In this case it seems that ε is stable when forming out of the melt in a Sn rich melt (CuSn37), also at room temperature. However, it was never observed in the present studies forming due to annealing in a temperature range of 400 °C due to solid-solid transformation which is in good agreement with literature [1, 5]. Therefore the recent study confirms that the formation of the ε-phase can be ignored for industrial processes. #### Acknowledgement This work is financially supported by the Austrian Christian-Doppler Research Society and Wieland Werke, Vцhringen for which the authors kindly acknowledge. **Keywords:** Tin bronzes, thermodynamics, ternary, solidification, casting, macrosegregation 

#### Abstract 

The paper discusses simulation results for columnar solidification of ternary bronze alloys in continuous casting of rectangular casting geometries. Thermodynamics of Cu-Sn-P is included by using spline-interpolation techniques to model the liquidus surface and the solubil

ity of Sn and P in the different phases. The applied volume-averaged solidification model considers two interpenetrating continua, i.e. the melt as the primary phase and columnar dendrites as the secondary phase. At the interface it is distinguished explicitly between interface and average concentrations. The formation of columnar dendrites is approximated by growing cylinders. After their formation at the mold/metal interface, they are considered to move continuously with the applied casting speed. The velocity field of the melt flow is obtained by solving the momentum conservation equation and within the mushy zone we consider hydrodynamic interaction between melt and solid and local formation of microsegregation. This solidification model is applied to a laboratory continuous casting process. The simulated liquid and solid concentrations are compared with ternary Scheil calculations and, in addition, the average mixture concentration of the simulation results is validated by experimental concentration measurements. 

#### 1 Introduction 

Bronzes and especially Phosphor bronzes are among the oldest engineering materials still used for many different applications. The most economical way to produce Phosphor bronze is DC casting. Figure 1 shows a schematic sketch of a vertical DC casting process. A vertical continuous casting machine consists mainly of the mold with a tundish or a melting furnace and the mechanicalhydraulic strand withdrawal mechanism. The melt is kept at casting temperature in the heated tundish from where it flows into the mold. The mold itself holds the melt and in addition extensively

cools it. This leads to the formation of a solidified shell at the beginning and finally to complete solidification of the strand. 



Figure 1: Schematic sketch of a vertical DC caster for bronze [1]. 

Since bronze is a metallic alloy with a solidification interval of about 200 K, depending on the alloy composition, during casting a region called mushy zone develops where both liquid melt and solidifying dendrites are present. Pronounced segregation takes place in bronzes because of the slow diffusion of Sn in the solid and the wide solidification interval. Figure 2 shows a typical microstructure observed in vertical DC casting of bronze just after casting without any heat treatment. On the left side the phase distribution at an outer boundary is shown whereas on the right the microstructure in the centre of the casting is displayed. The location of both micrographs is indicated schematically in the middle part of Figure 2. It is obvious that the microstructure at the centre is finer with less α-δ eutectoid compared to the outer boundary region. Measurements reveal that tin content at the outer boundary is highest and gradually decreases towards the centre. This concentration inhomogeneity is often referred to as macrosegregation which forms due to

microsegregation combined with relative motion between the liquid and the dentrite in the mushy zone. Figure 3 shows such a profile as measured by industry. Since it is not possible to remove this macroscopic concentration inhomogeneity by heat treatment, it is of great importance to reduce its formation directly during casting. Since the pioneer work of Kaufman and Bernstein in 1970 [2], calculations of phase diagrams have become a widely used tool for predicting thermodynamic information by computational techniques. This method, known as the CALPHAD method (CALculation of PHAse Diagrams) [3, 4], enables the prediction of phase evolution and of corresponding solidification paths by taking into account different cooling rates, back diffusion and/or coarsening [5, 6, 7]. During the last years it was tried to improve the accuracy of macrosegregation prediction in DC casting of non-ferrous alloys by including thermodynamics of higher order systems. For example Eskin [8] discussed the formation of segregation for a ternary Al-alloy based on a two phase model for equiaxed solidification. He stated _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 66 _Macrosegregation Prediction for DC Casting of Ternary Bronze Alloys_ that direct coupling between thermodynamic calculations and CFD simulations might be rather time consuming, especially if an industrial size casting process is considered. Besides, improvements were done to numerically describe the formation of macrosegregation in DC casting of bronze [9, 10, 11]. To model such a solidification process conservation equations for mass, enthalpy and solute were considered on the macroscopic scale and thermodynamic equilibrium conditions on the liquid/solid interfacial microscale. Ludwig and co-workers proposed a method [10, 11] to couple thermodynamic data with a multiphase solidification model. Since direct coupling is rather time consuming, the coupling is done by providing access to thermodynamic data through linearization methods, splines or tabulation and interpolation techniques like ISAT (In-Situ Adaptive Tabulation) [12]. α+δ

#### 2 Model Description 

During solidification of continuous casting of bronze, equiaxed and/or columnar dendritic growth is observed depending on the applied casting conditions. A multiphase model for columnar and/or equiaxed solidification has been developed by Ludwig, Wu and co-workers from 2002 to 2007 [14-17]. For the simulations discussed in the present paper this model is applied whereas nucleation and growth of equiaxed grains are neglected. Flow phenomena like forced convection, shrinkage induced feeding flow as well as thermo-solutal convection, grain sedimentation or exudation, etc. have an impact on the macrosegregation distribution whereas microsegregation only depends on the thermodynamics of the special system. The thermodynamic information of Cu-Sn-P as published in [10-12] is included by coupling pre-calculated thermodynamic data with the multiphase model. In the recent paper splines of third order are used to model thermodynamics during solidification. Here, as a first attempt for the prediction of macrosegregation, just forced convection and shrinkage induced feeding flow, modelled by taking into account the density difference between liquid and solid, are applied. 

Figure 4 shows the liquidus surface of the Cu rich corner of the ternary phase diagram for Cu-Sn-P (based on calculations with Thermo-Calc) including different monovariant lines. In the calculation with the multiphase solidification code, the liquidus surface _TL_ and the concentration of the two alloying elements in the solid at the solid/liquid interface<sup>_c_~</sup> _cSn_ and<sup>_c_~</sup> _cP_<sup>are based on computational</sup> thermodynamics (Thermo-Calc). For the industrial application of the model these three thermodynamic functions are spline-interpolated over the whole area [12]. In general, solidification of bronze alloys starts with the formation of α dendrites. The black arrows in Figure 4 show an example of a solidification path (CuSn6P0.5) as proposed by a ternary Scheil calculation. Point _A_ indicates the initial alloy concentration whereas point B marks the end of solidification. During primary solidification the melt enriches and so the solidification path crosses the first peritectic groove at P1. Between P1 and the second peritectic groove P2 the melt forms β and between P2 and the eutectic groove E γ forms from the melt. In the eutectic groove E two binary eutectics, first γ + Cu3P and later β + Cu3P form. As soon as the concentration of the remaining melt fits to a concentration that corresponds to the eutectic groove, the binary eutectics form and the melt concentration follows the eutectic groove until it reaches the ternary eutectic point (B). There the formation of the ternary eutectic α + Cu3P + β finally terminates the solidification process. Note that, if back

#### 5 Summary 

Macrosegregations in DC casting are caused by a relative motion between solid and liquid during the solidification process. Thermodynamic data is included into solidification simulation with the software FLUENT by using spline-interpolation techniques to model the liquidus surface and the solubility of Sn and P in the different phases. The presented model was applied to a laboratory continuous casting process. 

Concluding the following is stated: 

- Ternary simulation based on nonlinear splines of the third order to approximate _TL_ ,<sup>_c_~</sup> _c Sn_ and _P_<sup>compared well with ternary Scheil calculations. Some deviations are observed due to the dif-</sup> 

- <sup>_c_~</sup> _c_ ference between the solidification model presented which is based on diffusion-controlled solidification kinetics and Scheil’s model which assumes infinite diffusion in the liquid. The position of the profile in the strand also has an influence on the macrosegeregation, which is mainly caused by the different flow conditions in the casting. 

- The predicted macrosegregation of Sn and P shows the same distribution pattern as observed in experimental investigations, namely positive at the wall and negative in the center of the strand. Up to now, quantitative agreement with the measurement was not fully obtained. One reason for that could be that the applied thermodynamic model is developed for modelling peritectic transformation in a ternary system but the eutectic transformation is not yet considered, and therefore the solidification has to be stopped at a certain point. Besides, just shrinkage induced feeding flow is applied in the presented model. Other flow phenomena may also influence the formation of macrosegregation. 

Based on the liquid and solid concentration of the ca

lculation microsegregation and macrosegregation can be predicted for the solidified strand. Further work should be performed to improve the model for the inclusion of the eutectic transformation and other convection phenomena.

### BB05xi and BB95 – Two New Environmental Friendly Copper Alloys 

Ralf Hojda, Dr. Michael Kцhler

**Keywords:** Copper alloys, bronze, CuFe2P, C19400, tin-coated, BB05xi, ecobronze, connector, C52400, BB95, CuSn10, bendability, miniaturization, recyclability, material cycle 

#### Abstract 

Soaring CO2 emissions, increasing environmental pollution and the depletion of resources are all calling for a reorientation towards sustainability in the development and production of materials and their composites. 

In the future, the selection of materials and material combinations will depend on their environmental compatibility to a much greater extent than in the past. Decisions based on mechanical and technological properties alone are being edged out and superseded by a holistic approach to the cycles of resources. 

This paper presents two new alloys with remarkable ecological and economic potentials: 

The first is a new phosphorus bronze – with a property profile identical to CuFe2P – which can be recycled directly even when tinned. The other is a high-strength phosphorus bronze whose properties support the trend towards miniaturization, making the material ideal in applications designed to save resources. 

#### 1 BB05xi 

The choice of material for electrical and electronic components is based primarily on physical criteria such as electrical conductivity, modulus of elasticity, thermal relaxation and processing characteristics, i.e. ductility and bendability, and welding behaviour. Issues relating to partial or total surface protection are of secondary importance, alongside the basic availability of the materials and their prices. An examination of production and punching waste reveals that in many cases it is not given the attention that, on ecological and economic grounds, it deserves. This is illustrated by the following example.

Usually a small amount of phosphorus is added to alloys of this type for the purpose of deoxidation, which is why they are also referred to as phosphor bronzes. The properties of this group of alloys depend mainly on their tin and phosphorus content, and to a lesser extent on the other added alloy elements. By means of suitable processing, they can be adjusted for use in a wide range of applications. The many industrial applications for these alloys range from high quality connectors and sockets for electronic modules to electrically conductive contact springs. In the past, “downgrading” used to be carried out as an efficient method of selecting a phosphor bronze. In other words, the technological properties of a low-alloy phosphor bronze were adjusted so that its spring characteristics and processing properties corresponded to those of the original high-alloy phosphor bronze. However, certain constraints had to be taken into consideration: The tin and phosphorus content influence the work hardening behaviour and ductility of phosphor

Another reason to do so was the demand for miniaturisation of connectors, as a reduction in cross section reduces the contact force at constant deflection of the spring element. For a defined constant force, therefore, the spring element has to be redesigned – the design stress increases accordingly. One solution for this is the newly developed alloy BB95, a 10 % phosphor bronze: 

At a yield stress level Rp0.2 > 720 MPa, the bendability of BB95 in BW90° R/S is superior to that of an 8 % tin bronze by a factor of 2. Depending on the intended application, BB95 can be hardened to a yield stress level Rp0.2 of 800 MPa, and the high-strength variety to >950 MPa. 

The difference in electrical conductivity between BB95 and an 8 % tin bronze is approx. 1 % IACS, i.e. the tin has a negligible conductivity-reducing influence when present in the alloy at this level. At SH (spring hard) temper, BB95 exhibits the same softening properties as an 8 % phosphor bronze; a significant reduction in hardness is first observed at about 280 °C. 

In addition, the relaxation of the new material (< 20 % at a temperature of 100 °C for test duration of 10,000 h) is comparable to that of the above mentioned reference alloy (provided the stress level is identical). 

Given the above mentioned contact force, these results suggest that it should be possible to achieve a reduction in the thickness of the material, and therefore a reduction of about 20 % in the amount of material needed, by using BB95. Converted into CO2 savings, and taking into account the scraps typically arising in the production of alloys, the potential thus obtainable for 1000 tonnes per annum amounts to about 200 tonnes, corresponding to the yearly emissions from about 100 households. 

#### 3 Summary 

Saving resources, reducing CO2 emissions and keeping the environment clean will in future take top priority in the development and production of materials and composite materials. The economic and ecological potentials of the newly developed BB05xi alloy provide an excellent example of the advantages attainable compared with the CuFe2P alloy which is still widely used in many technical applications. Since there is no need for indirect recycling of tinned base material, CO2 emissions as well as electric energy and acid consumption will be significantly reduced. 

Achieving a decisive contribution towards miniaturization through the use of h

igh-strength alloys is demonstrated by the development of a new 10 % phosphorus bronze. Compared with an 8 % copper-tin alloy, this opens up new avenues to cutting back on resources in the use of materials. Savings of up to 20 % are possible.

### Machinability and Mechanical Properties of LeadFree Wrought Brass Alloys with Bismuth and Graphite Particles by Powder Metallurgy Process 

Dr. Imai Hisahi, Katsuyoshi Kondoh, Shufeng Li, Haruhiko Atsumi, Yoshiharu Kosaka Akimichi Kojima, Junko Umeda 

Joining and Welding Research Institute Osaka University 11-1 Mihogaoka 

Ibaraki, Osaka, Japan 

**Keyword** : Cu-40Zn brass, lead-free, machinability, bismuth, graphite particles 

#### Abstract 

In this paper, the effect of bismuth and graphite particles in the brass alloy on its mechanical properties and machinability was quantitatively evaluated to develop the machinable lead-free brass produced by a powder metallurgy (P/M) process. Cu-40Zn brass alloy powders containing bismuth were produced as matrix materials by a rapid solidification process, and graphite particles were used as raw additives to the Cu-40Zn brass alloy powders. Bismuth were uniformly dispersed as particles in the matrix of the as-received brass alloy powders, and appeared at the brass powder surface during heat treatment above their melting point. After consolidation of the elemental mixture of the brass alloy powder containing bismuth and graphite particles via spark plasma sintering and hot extrusion process, the bismuth and graphite particles existed independently in the matrix. The synergy effect of bismuth and graphite particles on the mechanical improvement and machinability of the brass alloys was very effective, compared to the brass including only one of the above machinable elements. The addition of 0.5 wt. % graphite particles and 2.2 wt. % bismuth in P/M extruded brass alloys resulted in an excellent machinability comparable to that of the conventional brass alloy with lead. Shaping the machined chips depended on the brass powder bonding and the distribution of machinable particles. 

#### 1 Introduction 

Cu-Zn alloys (brasses) are widely used as industrial materials because of their excellent characteristics such as high corrosion resistance, non-magnetism, good machinability and hot forgeability. The conventionally commercialized machinable brass alloys contain 2-5 % lead, assisting their machi- 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

89 

_Imai, Kondoh, Li, Atsumi, Kosaka, Kojima, Umeda_ 



nability [1, 2]. However, it is necessary to reduce the content of the lead in the material from the viewpoint of its hazardous effects on the environment and humans [3, 4]. The addition of bismuth (Bi), silicon (Si), selenium (Se), and graphite to brass alloys as alternative elements to lead addition has been discussed to improve machinability [5-7]. Furthermore, graphite particles, which are common solid lu

bricant and have significant effect of friction reduction [6, 7] are available to be used as additives to brass alloys because they are cheap and environmentally benign [8]. It is, however, very difficult to uniformly disperse graphite particles in the brass matrix by an ingot metallurgy (I/M) process due to the significantly large difference in density between graphite and brass alloy, and to the floating of graphite by adhering to vaporized zinc (Zn) in heating and casting [9]. In the case of Bi, its content dissolved in copper is 0.5 wt. %, similar to lead, and the adverse effect on the human body from Bi is small. However, Bi aggregate at the grain boundaries, and exist ununiformly in the casted brass ingot. Therefore, the machinability of brass with Bi is inferior to the conventional alloy with lead [10], and cracks are easily generated from Bi particles as the secondary dispersed phase. In this paper, the effect of both Bi and graphite particles in the brass alloy on its mechanical properties and machinability was quantitatively evaluated to develop the machinable lead-free brass produced by powder metallurgy (P/M) process. 

#### 2 Experimental procedure 

Cu-40Zn alloy powder containing Bi was prepared by water atomization. It had a mean particle size of about 150 µm. The Bi additions to the brass alloy were 1.0 and 2.2 wt. %. When the P/M brass alloy contained 2.5 wt. % or more Bi, it showed less than 20 % of elongation [11]. Graphite, having a mean particle size of 5 µm, was prepared as a machinable element. Its addition to brass powder was 0, 0.25, and 0.5 wt. %. The elemental mixture of the atomized brass powder containing Bi and the graphite particles was prepared by dry blending. 

Three kinds of billets were prepared for the extrusion, namely by spark plasma sintering (SPS), by green compaction and by casting. SPS (SPS SYNTEX INC., SPS-1030) was used to consolidate the above elemental mixture powders. The consolidation of the high-density sintered compact was performed using a temperature of 1053 K for 30 min. under 40 MPa pressure in vacuum [12]. Green compaction was employed by applying a pressure of 600 MPa at room temperature by using a hydraulic press machine (2000 kN SHP-200-450: SHIBAYAMAKIKAI Co.). Cast ingot billets with the same Bi content and without graphite particles were prepared for extrusion as a comparison. 

Each billet was preheated at 873 K for 180 s in Ar gas atmosphere using a heating rate of 0.65 K/s in a muffle furnace (KDF S-70: DENKEN Co.). Then, it was immediately extruded by using the hydraulic press machine applying an extrusion ratio of 37. 

The microstructural investigation by scanning electron microscopy (SEM, JSM-6500F: JEOL) equipped with X-ray energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS EX-64175JMU: JEOL) was carried out on the consolidated specimens to observe the morphology and distribution of machinable particles.

Mechanical properties of extruded materials were evaluated by a tensile testing machine (Autograph AG-X 50 kN: SHIMADZU) under a strain rate of 5Ч10<sup>-4</sup> s<sup>-1</sup> . The investigation of fractured surfaces of the tensile test specimens were carried out by using SEM. The machinability of Cu-40Zn brass alloys was evaluated by a drilling test using a drill tool (EX-SUS-GDS: OSG Co.) of 4.5 mm diameter under dry conditions. The rotation speed of the drill was 900 rpm, and the applied load during drilling was 9.8 N. The drilling time to produce a hole of 5 mm depth was measured. After repeating this drilling test 10 times, the average drilling time was used as machinability parameter.

Copper rod is produced by means of continuous processes since the early 1960s. Looking at the wide scope of different manufacturing processes along the whole value chain from copper production down to the OEMs and the growing reams of applications these basic definitions alone are not sufficient any more. Therefore additional agreements between producer and processors focusing on specific applications are necessary. This should be demonstrated looking at the example of different microstructures of copper rod in the as-delivered condition.

If both kinds of copper rod are introduced to real industrial forming processes, the described effects could be much more relevant: Looking at cold rolling of net shape direct cast rod, its coarse grains could cause rough surfaces and cracks at the edges and along the rim zones of the flat wire. Predrawing combined with additional thermal treatment to achieve an annealed microstructure before the cold rolling could be a solution here. In case of cold drawing it could be helpful to adjust the process parameters accordingly when changing the feedstock. Net shape direct cast rod could need reduced drawing speed to avoid premature breakage. Moreover, a modified drawing calibration together with optimised inner geometries of the drawing dies could improve the drawing results in terms of quality and efficiency. These effects caused by the microstructure itself could be boosted by the fact that direct cast rod comes without any surface protection agents in contrast to rod produced by integrated processes. Therefore no additional lubrication effects between rod and die or rod and roll achieved by the organic protection layer itself could be expected. In total view the simple quasi-static tensile test has revealed already important differences in relevant characteristics of the respective rods in spite of their extensive similarity. With the change of the rod production process from integrated casting and rolling to net shape direct casting not only the oxygen content was reduced, but also a complete different microstructure in the as-delivered condition was introduced influencing the further processing of the rod significantly. #### 3

Copper rod for signal conductors 3.1 Demands 

Currently nearly all metallic conductors in car wire harnesses for power and signal transfer are drawn out of copper rod with a starting diameter of d = 8 mm. The absolute dominant copper grade is Cu-ETP1 [11]. Today only a very limited amount of special components like battery cables are partially substituted by aluminium to save weight. Further substitution by aluminium in car wire harnesses is not a major topic due to the needed greater sections, the different behaviour in drawing and joining and also due to the specific demands concerning structural durability and recycling. Moreover it has to be stated, that also Flexible Flat Cables (FFC) made out of cut copper strip and/or rolled predrawn copper wire are until today only used in very limited parts of the harnesses and have not gained the importance expected some years ago [12].

About 2 to 4 kg copper conductor mass in a typical car wire harness is needed to transfer signals. Different OEMs specify individual demands for the respective components of the harness. The following data are therefore just indications, which differ depending on the specific producer: For signal transmission the conductors do not necessarily need highest conductivity, as only low amounts of energy are needed. Therefore the minimal diameter of the conductor is defined by the tensile strength and the resulting tensile force of the stranded wire, which should exceed Fmin=70 N to avoid breakage during manufacturing and installation of the car wire harness. At the same time the elongation at breakage should indicate enough ductility to achieve sufficient flexibility of the harness during the installation. Demands on conductivity vary depending on the respective specifications between κ=22 % IACS and κ= 80 % IACS. Moreover different other demands are defined by the OEMs: Proven structural durability of the whole system in a temperature range from -50 °C up to 120 °C, in some cases 150 °C, for a period of 3000 h. Independent from that the respective signal wire must show full process capability with the existing manuf

acturing technologies (e.g. drawing, insulating and joining) and the respective machinery [14]. Today the bulk of Cu-ETP1 conductors for signal transmission in car wire harnesses come as stranded wires. The cross sections vary from s = 0.35 mm2 to s = 0.5 mm2 to fulfil the combinations of demands. The respective copper amount in the EU for the signal transfer in car wire harnesses was estimated in the year 2007 with 55,000 t/y rod. With the growing activities of the automotive industry to save _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 107 _Jacobsen_ mass and therefore to reduce cross sections of the conductors actually alternative conductor materials are sought after. ##### 3.2 Scope of the program Aurubis AG has set up an investigation program to identify and develop suitable copper rod grades taking also into consideration the subsequent manufacturing stages. Rod production trials with suitable micro alloyed copper grades and copper alloys as well as subsequent experiments with wires drawn out of the produced rod samples were carried out. The rod production itself has been performed in industrial scale mostly on the rod line displayed in Figure 3 to achieve realistic conditions from the beginning. Other rod samples were produced in the operations of Aurubis in Olen and Stolberg also under real shop floor conditions. Table 1 supplies an overview about the scope of the investigated copper grades and copper alloys. All rod samples came in a diameter of d = 8 mm in annealed condition to eliminate any potential negative effects during the following trials and tests. As the rod samples in the grades Cu-ETP1 and CuAg0.1 out of the Southwire process show an annealed microstructure due to the integrated hot rolling (see Figure 5), no additional treatments were necessary here. The rod samples in the grade CuMg0.2 have been net shape direct cast by upwards casting process and subsequently been extruded via the Conform process to a diameter of d = 8 mm achieving also an annealed microstructure. The brass rod samples in the grade Ms 37 have been hot extruded out of cast billets with subsequent cold drawing. ###### 3.3.5 Evaluation 

None of the investigated grades and alloys was able to meet all specified demands of the OEMs for new metallic signal conductors in car harnesses to the full extent. The best results until now were delivered by cold drawn wires CuAg0.1 and CuMg0.2. Brass is not considered as a real option due to complete different manufacturing technologies and workflows inducing higher specific system costs not suitable for the mass production of stranded signal conductors. 

Taking all decision factors into account like the capability of the copper, specific production costs, process compatibility and sufficient recycling structures and possibilities, in total view a relative preference for stranded signal conductors out of grade CuAg0.1 could be identified. Indeed the thermal stability of this binary micro alloy is not fully satisfactory until now. 

In the meantime Aurubis has started a second program of trials with newly designed copper micro alloys.

The basic precondition to increase the coil weight is the understanding and optimisation of the coiling process in the rod line itself. It must be mentioned that the speed of the 8 mm rod to be coiled reaches about 35 m/s. Therefore computer based simulations have been modelled and performed with different spinner pipe geometries. After some iteration modified spinner pipes together with additional peripheries have been introduced. Moreover it has been necessary to modify and strengthen the reusable wooden pallets to maintain the safety of transport and the durability of the pallets. The anonymous on stock production meeting just the demands specified in the common standards has been advanced often to a production on order: Nowadays the inventories of typical rod operations contain up to 200 different rod products, which are assigned at a large extent to certain customers. Processability and quality of the final products are already influenced by the rod production process itself even if the demands of the respective standards and norms are continuously met. Independent from that the increasing demands of the OEMs influence the copper rod production more and more, which was shown using the example of actual developments of copper grades for sign

#### Abstract 

Rapid development of electronics and electrical engineering imposes a necessity to search for new materials enabling fast and lossless transmission of electrical signals. Increasingly common application of electronic systems and elements of electrical engineering contributed to the development of a new group of products representing highly advanced properties. Modern solutions concerning the materials to be used for manufacturing of the above specified products concentrate mainly on high purity copper. As a standard Oxygen Free Copper (OFC) or high purity Oxygen Free High Conductivity Copper (OFHC) are used for production of this kind of wires. OFHC copper purity class of 4N (99.99 %) - contains approximately 1-3 ppm of oxygen and the total amount of impurities on the level not exceeding 22 ppm. This type of copper is additionally characterized by excellent deformation capabilities as well as corrosion and hydrogen embrittlement resistance. 

This article presents the analysis of the results of the complex research program on identification of the properties pertaining to wire rods produced oxygen free copper from UPCAST line and ETP wire rod produced on Contirod<sup></sup> line - in both cases the same type of cathode was used. Additionally, a subsequent analysis of the annealing susceptibility of wires obtained from Cu-OF rod (Upcast<sup>®</sup> ) and Cu-ETP wire rod (Contirod<sup></sup> ) was carried out. The comparative research on the recrystallization temperature proved to be the most interesting point. 

#### 1 Introduction 

The beginnings of high quality cables characterized by lossless signal transmission (audio/video cables) manufacturing concept dates back to 1970s when oxygen-free copper (OF) was first manufactured. It is well-known that the quality of cables has a great impact on the quality of sound in audio systems, therefore replacing of poor quality cables by cables of high quality may considerably

improve sound quality. When such cables are used with AC current, variable magnetic field is generated that creates resistance to AC current. The higher current frequency is the higher resistance is created. This phenomenon is called inductance. In case of cables when an isolated

wire is shaped in a form of a coil or positive and negative terminals, inductance is rising which reduces sound clearness. However, if isolated wires with positive and negative terminals are twisted like a rope or string, inductance is falling which results in better sound clearness. Generally speaking, if cables are twisted, inductance is falling while capacitance is rising which reduces frequency due to which sound becomes obscure. The quality of sound transmitted by wires depends first of all on chemical constitution of wires and moreover on the type of insulating material, crystal structure of wires, inductance, skin effect caused by thermal treatment and impedance between audio systems. As a standard Oxygen Free Copper (OFC) or high purity Oxygen Free High Conductivity Copper (OFHC) are used for production of this kind of wires. OFHC copper – purity class of 4N (99.99 %) - contains approximately 1-3 ppm of oxygen and the total amount if impurities on the level not exceeding 22 ppm. This type of copper is additionally characterized by excellent deformation capabilities as well as corrosion and hydrogen embrittlement resistance. 

In electronics the most commonly used are the types of oxygen free copper with suitably shaped grains and with the lowest possible number of grains per single length unit. Long Grain Copper (LGC) and Long Crystal Copper (LCC) are the examples of the applied solutions. In case of those two types of copper the number of grains per unit is reduced to the level of 200 grains in one meter of length. LGC and LCC in this respect outrank OF copper, in which the number of grains reaches the level of approximately 500/mb. Copper obtained in Ohno Continuous Casting technology – OCC – demonstrates properties similar to those of LGC and LCC copper. The main purpose of application of this type of technology is the reduction of the number of crystals in a conductor. In case of highly specialized applications, e.g. in electron devices, (elements of electron accelerators, cryogenics) the 6N class copper with the purity of 99.99997 % is used and it is referred to as _functionally perfect copper_ **(FPC)** . At present, the purest type of copper obtained on industrial scale is the material of 8N purity class (99.999999 %). High quality cables are often produced with the use of 6- 7N purity class copper. Such advanced properties cannot be provided by the traditionally used ETP copper whose oxygen content ranges between 200-600 ppm. Selection of the products obtained with the use of oxygen free copper is rather wide and it concentrates mainly on the highly advanced products. By temperatures lower than 380 °C the CuO compound is formed and by temperatures higher than 380 °C Cu2O is formed. The content of oxygen usually ranges between 200 and 600 ppm. The lack of oxygen in oxygen free copper constitutes the main factor contributing to the improvement of its plasticity, electrical conductivity, corrosion and hydrogen embrittlement resistance as compared to the ETP copper. The content of oxygen below 3 ppm prevents formation of CuO and Cu2O, which hamper the drawing process of wire rods below 0.1 mm in diameter [9]. The presence of copper oxides leads to the decrease of corrosion resistance and makes thermal treatment of the material in the reduction atmosphere impossible.
