#### 3 Methods of production of oxygen free copper 

While the production of ETP copper seems to be under control from the technological point of view, in case of oxygen free copper the application of highly advanced manufacturing techniques is required. Production of ETP copper rod to be used for electrical purposes is dominated by two methods of continuous melting, casting and rolling: Contirod<sup>®</sup> and Southwire SCR<sup>®</sup> . However, they do not provide a possibility to obtain the oxygen free copper. One of the most modern methods enabling production of oxygen free copper feedstock destined for further processing with the application of the method of micro-wires drawing is Upcast<sup>®</sup> technology developed by Outokumpu company, which is based on the continuous simultaneous realization of the cathodes melting operation cycle, oxygen reduction and oxygen free copper (OFC) up casting in the form of coiled wires. 

High purity copper cathodes CATH-1 (Grade A) are used as the feedstock and they undergo the process of continuous melting in the induction furnace. According to ASTMB170 standard the total content of impurities in CATH-1 copper cathodes should not exceed 25 ppm. At the next stage of the production cycle, liquid copper undergoes de-oxidation process. The role of de-oxidizing agent is played by Fe and S reduced charcoal the layer of which covers the surface of the liquid copper. The process of the metal solidification takes place in a special vertical crystallizer submerged in liquid copper. The solidified ingot is further pulled up at a specific velocity by means of drawing rollers and finally coiled with the system of coilers. The above described technology enables production of oxygen free copper wires characterized by high conductivity and plasticity with the range of diameters from 8 to 24 mm at the speed of 4 m/min (for the diameter of 8 mm) which makes it possible to achieve the average annual production output of approximately 1500 tons. 

Oxygen free copper is also produced by means of other methods such as: Rautomead<sup>®</sup> , Conticast<sup>®</sup> or Ohno<sup>®</sup> . Figure 4 presents the macrostructure of the cast oxygen free copper rod – 8 mm in diameter. It can be seen that the structure is formed by two types of grains: the first – small regularly shaped grains of the cast core, and the second – elongated, large dendrites perpendicular to the ingot axis.

#### 4 The objectives of the study, the research program, materials 

The main aim of this study was to determine the influence of the diversities in the initial condition of the feedstock on the development of the properties of wires obtained in the cold working processes. The study comprises two research objectives: 

1. Determination of the influence of the wire rod condition on the material work-hardening in the course of the drawing process. 

2. Determination of the influence of the wire rod condition on the changes in wire recrystallization temperature. 

Finding the solution to the so formulated research problem required a series of well-planned tests to be conducted on Cu-ETP and OFC rods. Also a new method of their analysis needed to be developed. In particular the program comprised researches on the processes of drawing and recrystallization constituting two basic technological operations referring to the rod production process and deciding about the final properties of wires destined for the use in electronics. ### Research of Silver Copper from Contirod and Upcast Lines for the Production of Trolley Wires 

T. Knych, A. Kawecki, A. Mamala, P. Kwaśniewski 

AGH-University of Science and Technology Al. Mickiewicza 30 Cracow, Poland 

**Keywords:** Oxygen free silver copper, CuAg0.10, trolley wire, Upcast<sup>®</sup> , Contirod<sup>®</sup> 

#### Abstract 

This paper presents the results of comparison tests of the mechanical and electrical properties of type AC-150 trolley wires, made from CuAg0.10 silver copper grade. Continuous cast and rolled a rods made by the Contirod method and rods made from continuous vertical casting line with the Upcast method – were the ingredient material for the wire production. 

The method of processing input material into a trolley wire is described more precisely, in industrial production circumstances, the scheme of material deformation and technological parameters of drawing process are presented. The results of technological tests have been assessed to discover any latent defects in the material, which may occur while drawing the trolley wires. 

#### 1 Introduction 

The inclusion of Polish railway lines into the European system of transport corridors, made it necessary to update and adapt building infrastructure as well as railway rolling stock. The Polish railway electrical supply system is based on a voltage of 3 kV DC, causing a significantly heavier current loading of the network due to high running speeds and increasingly heavier transported goods. Because of this, the newly-developed or modernized railway lines need be built using applied modern construction and material solutions. The trolley wires, which transfer electrical energy from the substations to the locomotive motors, are one of the most important components of a railway network. Electrical current is collected from the network using the slipping plates on a pantograph located on top of the locomotive. 

Higher running speed and increase in the weight of transported goods results in the need for increasing electrical power tran

sferred through a trolley network. In particular, in low-voltage systems of

The largest task in solving the problem of collecting current from a traction network with a high running speed is to ensure that the network is equipped with the correct conducting elements, including low abrasion trolley wires and contact strips on current collectors [4]. 

#### 2 Characteristics of trolley wires 

A trolley wire operates within variable stresses. Although forces applied to the wire are constant, its cross-sections are gradually reduced through wear and tear, and the tension stress value changes. Cyclic, short-term thermal effects result from friction (contact strips of electric current collector against the trolley wire) and localised heating of material (different the currents flow effects) [4]. This area is the most essential part of an electrical traction network when considering the energy transfer from sub-station to locomotive. 

During heavy operating trolley wires are heated to the extreme temperatures. Those temperatures are effect of Joule heating and friction energy. Due to those facts high electrical conductivity, creep, stress relaxation, fatigue, wear resistance and thermal stability of material are required. Adequate material properties have economic repercussions for line maintenance. 

Extensive research has been conducted in recent years by AGH university in the field of silvercopper trolley wires, which has resulted in the development and implementation of manufacturing for trolley wires of the type DjpS100 (AC-100) grade CuAg0.10 [1, 3]. 

These wires have superior usable properties when compared with traditional wires made from copper of the same cross-section. Trolley wires of the type AC-100 grade CuAg0.10 have about 8 % better mechanical properties, 20 % better creep properties, have a recrystallization temperature which is about 150 °C higher, 25 % lower friction ratio and 45 % lower wear with simultaneously maintained high electrical conductivity. This is close to the conductivity of trolley wires of the type AC-100 made from copper grade ETP (the difference being a mere 1.4 %). These properties make DjpS100 wires an excellent substitute for the Djp100 wires which have already been installed in Polish traction networks. DjpS100 wires (AC-100, grade CuAg0.10) are designed for railway lines with a high running speed, carrying heavy goods and heavy vehicles, as well municipal tram lines with high intensity traffic [3]. 

However a trolley wire AC-100, made from silver-copper has not sufficient a cross-section (100 mm<sup>2</sup> ) for the newly constructed traction networks with a current loading capacity of over 2.5 kA due to overheating. Therefo

re, on a performance basis and because of its impressive material properties, work on production technology of trolley wires made from silver-copper of larger crosssection, in example 150 mm<sup>2</sup> has begun [2, 5].

#### 3 Materials for the tests 

Tests were carried out on trolley wires made from silver-copper grade CuAg0.10 (type DjpS150) with a cross-section of 150 mm<sup>2</sup> made from rod produced on a Contirod line and wires produced from an Upcast line rod. 

Trolley wires of the type AC-150 (Figure 1b) have been manufactured using an industrial method at Cracovian Cable Works TELE-FONIKA Kable Sp. z o.o. S.K.A. The drawing line (shown in Figure 1a) installed at the cable works plant, consists of the following sub-assemblies: horizontal, fivestage line-drawing machine HENRICH Model HTH-05-01-SL, horizontal, crosswise movable (oscillating) traverse winder HENRICH Model GSO-1600-G-N-HY together with single winder with cross winding of a wire. 

During wire drawing cross-section of material is gradually reduced in dies. Initially circular crosssection of rod changes to final trolley cross-section. 

As it is being drawn for the purpose of trolley wire production, the input material gradually passes through a reduced circular cross-section until it is the correct diameter – governed by the profile drawing units which simultaneously change it into the required trolley shape. Controlling input material deformation is a delicate process because the gradual cutting of a cross-section into a trolley wire shape results in an increase of the process forces and increasing on stress heterogeneity and deformation of the cross-section of drawn-metal. As a result, metal and tool temperatures increase, which can lead to change of thermal state of a multi-drawing system and maybe causes a decrease of the finished product mechanical properties (dynamic recovery and recrystallization).

The method of silver copper rod production is important parameter and results in the level of mechanical and electrical properties of the finished product. The subject of this research paper, the trolley wires, have been manufactured by a drawing method of similar deformation program, where the strain hardening level was different. Upcast technology is different from the Contirod method; one property of Upcast technology is a high chemical purity of material and radically limited oxygen contents, thus enabling the material to attain far better electrical properties. The second difference is absence of plastic deformation of material in Upcast line while in Contirod method cast material is hot rolled. Upcast is a specific technology based on the continuous solidification of liquid metal, leading to achieving the typical casting structure with big columnar crystals. Contirod is a technology of continuous copper casting and rolling which produce fine recrystallized grains (compare Figure 5). As shown in the earlier tests, CuAg0.10 OFC materials, in relation to silver copper produced on a Contirod line, record a higher re-crystallization temperature and higher electrical conductivity, because of a limited oxide content and summarized by lower numbers of the grain boundaries. #### 5 Conclusions 

According to the tests results on the mechanical, electrical and s thermal stability properties of trolley wires AC-150 made from silver copper CuAg0.10 grade and produced on Upcast and Contirod lines – we can confirm the following. 

Trolley wires made from silver copper produced in continuous casting and rolling (CuAg0.10) and produced in directional casting (CuAg0.10 OFC) show that mechanical/electrical properties meet the requirements of railway branch standards. The technical tests showed no wire material defects which could have occurred in the drawing line. 

Radically limiting the oxygen contents in silver copper grade CuAg0.10 OFC and a summarized lower number of the grain boundaries results in an enhancement of the material recrystallization temperature, thus ensuring better mechanical properties. It was confirmed that the trolley wires made from silver copper grade OFC will retain their mechanical properties up to about 30 °C higher temperature in comparison with the wires made of silver copper, produced on a Contirod line, independently of the annealing time in various temperature between 1, 10 and 100 h.

#### Abstract 

The intense development of the world’s energy supply in recent years necessitates a continual demand to search for new materials and technological processes of constructions of components with higher and higher mechanical/electrical properties, that are used as conducting components in various branches of technology. Copper is a material generally used for connecting elements; it has a high electrical conductivity but relatively low mechanical properties and therefore cannot often be used in components which carry electrical/mechanical loads. To improve the mechanical properties of copper, it is alloyed with elements such as nickel, magnesium and zirconium but this has the effect of greatly reducing its electrical advantages. The alloy CuNi2Si is one material that can generally be used for current connections, its properties can be shaped through a thermal-plastic treatment. A die forging with simultaneous super-saturation is one of the highly effective technologies of CuNi2Si alloy processing for current conducting connections that have strong mechanical/electrical properties. This paper explains the construction of equipment for rail networks of high mechanical/current carrying capacities, its numerical analysis with regard to stress distribution and manufacturing technology – i.e. the parameters of the forging process and selection of heat treatment parameters. The paper also includes results of the tests and the operating properties of the holders and connectors made in this way. 

#### 1 Introduction 

Recent, intense development of world’s energy supply network gives rise to the continual search for new materials and technologies for their processing and production. The use of the right raw material combined with the development of the best production techniques is a sure indicator, that components produced in this way will have useful, advantageous pre-defined qualities. Our modern, fast-paced life means that we all want to travel faster and more comfortable – and this in turn gives

Traction network electrical supply systems, all over the world, are based on direct or alternating current and as current carrying elements, they require, materials with particularly high operating properties - among other things mechanical, electrical, anticorrosive and rheological [1

The geometry of trolley wires and carrying lines is predefined work on them entails the search for new technological solutions while the traction equipment in the form of various connections and clamps is subjected to the continuous evolution of new technological, material and constructional advances [2-3]. The purpose of these technological searches is to design equipment with better mechanical properties, higher skidding force of the current-carrying elements, lower transition resistance, high resistance to crawling and relaxation of tensions, high corrosive resistance and low weight. Copper and its alloys – these popular materials are used for current carrying elements on account of their electrical properties and the fact that copper oxide which forms on its surface is not a barrier while conducting the current. Most important current connections are made from copper of grade CuETP, mechanical holders are made of CuAl10Fe3Mn2 alloy, mechanical/electrical clamps are made from the CuNi2Si alloy. The technologies of their production are partially based on plastic working (i.e. forging, pressing) and partially on pressure and metal-mould casting. Mechanical/electrical requirements are particularly high in networks supplied with current voltage (e.g. 3 kV), because of high currents of about 4 kA, received by the electric locomotive. Too low electric conductivity of the equipment may result in overheating of the clamps and connections, therefore severely degrading their structural integrity, lowering of contact resistance and acceleration of rheological processes. As a consequence, it could lead to a network failure. Because of the lack of a good solution in equipment designed for highly mechanically/current loaded networks supplied with voltage of 3 kV, a team of scientists from AGH-University of Science and Technology and the Production Company Kuca designed a new form of traction equipment, selected the material and de-

#### 1 Introduction 

Based on today’s requirements of the industry to save resources and work environmentally friendly continuous heat treatment processes with high efficiency have become more and more important. 

In the following the process of inductive melting and casting as well as established continuous heat treatment routines with a successional forming process for semi finished products e.g. round and flat wire or narrow band will be discussed and compared. 

Following a short overview of the physical fundamentals the techniques listet below and their installation size and performance range as well as their advan

tages and disadvantages will be examined. - Cylindrical coil / heating in longitudinal field - Toroidal core coil / transformer - EE-core / heating in cross field #### 2 Physical Basics Theory of inductive heating is based mainly on Maxwell’s equations and Faraday’s law. Electric and magnetic field are inseparably bound together. Every electromagnetic primary field initiates a secondary field and so on. Respective electrical and magnetic field vectors are orthogonal to each other, primary and secondary field are directed in opposing directions. With a alternating magnetic field it is possible to achieve a contactless transfer of energy into the workpiece or melt. With the advantage of small currents and high voltages over small diameters big amounts of power can be transferred. _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 173 _Menge_ From the superstructure electrical alternate circuits can be created which allow a simplified design of processing systems. Furthermore thermal dependencies of physical parameters like resistivity, permeability or specific warmth and thermal conductivity should be considered in system dimensioning. #### 3 Systems engineering ##### 3.1 crucible melting furnace Basis is the heating of the crucible (e.g. graphite) or crucible content via a magnetic field induced by a cylindrical coil. Due to magnetic forces additional movements occur which improve mixing conditions in the melt. Burn-off is low. This system is suitable for small loads or production with frequent alloy changes. Moran Copper Development Association, Inc. 260 Madison Avenue New York, NY, 10016, USA **Keywords:** Antimicrobial, copper alloys, indoor air quality, energy efficiency, sick building syndrome #### 1 Introduction Air temperature in offices, schools, residences, and almost all occupied buildings is typically regulated by a mechanical air handling system. These Heating, Ventilating and Air Conditioning (HVAC) units are comprised of fans, heat exchangers, drip pans, condenser coils, ductwork and other components essential to effective temperature control. HVAC system components operate in warm, dark, humid environments that are ideal for fungal, bacterial and viral growth and distribution. Pathogenic organisms breeding in air handling systems are easily disseminated through ductwork into office spaces, classrooms, and homes. Various studies by health and safety authorities such as the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) have determined that pathogens distributed by air handling systems can lead to a condition known as Sick Building Syndrome [2]. Poor indoor air quality can cause acute symptoms such as sore throat, ear and nasal infection, headache, and even pneumonia or life-threatening infections. The EPA strongly believes that Sick Building Syndrome is a leading cause of lost productivity in the workplace. The 1989 Report to Congress on Indoor Air Quality estimated that “tens of billions of dollars per year” are lost as a result [3]. The EPA also stated that “improvements in the indoor air environment may substantially increase employee morale and productivity” [3]. Research coordinated by the U.S. Copper Development Association (CDA) has provided a promising

approach for improving indoor air quality. Laboratory testing has shown that copper and copper alloy surfaces kills or inhibit fungi, bacteria, and viruses [5-11]. Recent work accepted for publication by Weaver, Michels and Keevil demonstrated that copper killed fungal spores ( _Aspergillus_ spp., _Fusarium_ spp., _Penicillium chrysogenum_ , and _Candida albicans_ ) while aluminum and other solid surfaces had no effect [9]. Copper also prevented germination of spores, thereby reducing the risk of spore release (Figure 1). Biofilm colonization of _Legionella pneumophila_ was not supported 185 _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ _Michels, Estelle, Michel, Moran_ on copper surfaces, while it proliferated on plastic and steel surfaces. Therefore, replacing traditional HVAC materials such as heat exchanger fins and drip pans with copper alloy surfaces may have the potential to reduce biological contaminants that impact air quality [1]. Better air quality may lead to healthier working and living conditions which will reduce absenteeism and increase productivity. lead to healthier working and living conditions which will reduce absenteeism and increase produc-
tivity.
Figure 1: _Candida albicans_ viability on copper (C11000) and stainless steel (S30400) at 20 °C [9] In addition to health benefits, copper may also provide higher system energy efficiency for several reasons. First, copper has superior heat transfer properties compared to aluminum resulting in more efficient heat exchange. Second, copper has superior corrosion resistance to aluminum resulting in increased performance and product lifetime. The thick oxide layer that forms on aluminum heat exchanger fins can also restrict air flow which can reduce efficiency. Unlike copper, aluminum heat exchangers can develop biofilms that will reduce air flow, impede heat transfer, and increase energy usage. Higher efficiency obtained by using copper components may reduce energy consumption and lower operating costs [1]. To demonstrate the potential impact of copper HVAC components on indoor air quality and energy efficiency, several trials funded by the U.S. Department of Defense under the auspices of the Telemedicine and Advanced Technology Research Center (TATRC) are underway. 186 _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ _Antimicrobial Copper for Air Handling Systems_ #### 2 Laboratory Testing & Methodology ##### 2.1 General Air Quality Testing To best demonstrate the impact of copper on indoor air quality, a full-size, controllable air handling system was constructed at the University of South Carolina under the direction of Dr. Charles E. Feigley (Figure 2). The system draws outside air into the laboratory system and directs half through copper heat exchangers, and half through aluminum heat exchangers. Unfiltered air outside the laboratory used for testing contains sufficient fungal and bacterial concentrations needed to

demonstrate a meaningful reduction in airborne pathogens. Biological contaminants in the exit air from the copper and aluminum branches is collected on gelatin filters and is then plated, cultured, and quantified. Bacterial and fungal colony forming units detected in the exit air from both the copper and aluminum branches are analyzed to provide a side by side comparison of air quality. A more thorough description of the laboratory system has been published elsewhere [1].

##### 2.2 Biofilm Testing 

Additionally, small copper and aluminum coupons were inserted in between the fins of both the copper and aluminum heat exchangers. Coupons were removed progressively throughout the sampling periods and inspected for biofilm growth via standard culturing and scanning electron microscopy. 

##### 2.3 Condensate Testing 

Drip pans are another site for microbial growth in HVAC systems. Condensed water accumulated in drip pans can develop slime films and promote the growth and spread of pathogens. To combat this growth site, each copper heat exchanger was fitted with an all copper drip pan. The aluminum heat exchangers were fitted with aluminum drip pans for comparison. When condensate is available, water samples are taken and analyzed for the presence of bacteria and fungi. 

##### 2.4 Pilot Scale Testing 

While laboratory testing will provide substantial findings, it is equally important to demonstrate the effect of copper HVAC components in actual-use conditions. To observe the performance of copper heat exchangers and drip pans _in situ_ , a large scale test is underway at the Ft. Jackson military barracks in South Carolina. 

Two adjacent, fully functional and occupied barracks buildings are studied in this trial. The first building was retrofitted with all copper heat exchangers and drip pans, and the second building was retrofitted with new aluminum components to ensure an accurate comparison. A portable air sampling device is used to quantify the amount of fungal and bacterial colony forming units inside the buildings. Samples are taken from the “breathing zone” which is approximately head level, as well as the exit air in close proximity to the ceiling vents. As fungi and bacteria in the air are drawn through the sampler, the organisms are trapped on a gelatin membrane filter located within the device. The filter is removed after the sampling period, and organisms trapped on the filter are plated, cultured and enumerated in the laboratory. 

In each barracks building, an electronic control system is used to control heating and cooling cycles and also monitors and logs system energy consumption. This data will be used to compare the energy efficiency of the copper system building and the aluminum system building. 

The ongoing Ft. Jackson trials will provide long term data conc

erning the effect of copper HVAC components on biological contaminants that impact indoor air quality over both heating and cooling cycles. The Ft. Jackson results will indicate how copper systems might perform in other buildings such as schools, office buildings and residences.

#### 3 Conclusion 

In summary, Sick Building Syndrome is a well documented phenomenon and a significant cause of lost funds and serious health problems. Laboratory research, in conjunction with the trials at the University of South Carolina and Ft. Jackson, suggests that replacing traditional HVAC components with copper equivalents can reduce biological contaminants that impact indoor air quality, increase energy efficiency, lower operational costs, and benefit human health.

### Antimicrobial Regulatory Testing for Copper Alloys in the USA 

Ph.D. Harold T. Michels, Adam A. Estelle, James H. Michel, Wilton R. Moran 

Copper Development Association, Inc. 260 Madison Avenue New York, NY, 10016, USA 

**Keywords:** Antimicrobial, copper alloys, public health registration, laboratory practices testing 

#### Abstract 

Several bacteria known to be human pathogens die when they come in contact with copper and copper alloy surfaces. The amount of live bacteria drops by several orders of magnitude, to zero, on copper alloys within two hours. In contrast, almost no reduction is seen in the concentration of live organisms on stainless steel after several hours and even days. Aluminum, painted and coated surfaces, plastics, and most other touch surface materials also have no effect on pathogens. In addition, commercial coatings and other surfaces claiming to be antimicrobial show little to no reduction of bacteria in typical indoor environments. These results suggest that selecting copper alloys for environmental surfaces exposed to human touch can supplement infection control practices by reducing bacterial contamination. In order to make antimicrobial public health claims in the United States, the approval of the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is required. The EPA-required efficacy testing is described and the test results are summarized. The EPA officially registered 275 copper alloys (minimum copper content of 65 %) on February 29, 2008 as public health materials. On July 12, 2009, an additional registration was granted lowering the allowable copper content to 60 %. It is anticipated that regulatory approval will facilitate the introduction of antimicrobial copper alloys in hospitals, nursing homes and other healthcare facilities, as well as schools, and public buildings. Some of the market barriers to the healthcare industry are also mentioned. 

#### 1 Introduction 

Copper as a metal and in alloys has many useful characteristics which account for its continuing wide use. These include high thermal and electrical conductivity, good corrosion resistance, and ease of formability. However, one attribute has been forgotten and overlooked in recent times, its antimicrobial property.

Man exploited the antimicrobial attri

butes of copper before the nineteenth century, when Louis Pasteur developed his germ theory of disease in which infections are attributed to microbes invading the human body. Hippocrates, who was deemed the father of medicine, wrote the Hippocrates Collection, 460 to 380 B.C., that recommends the use of copper for leg ulcers related to varicose veins. Pliny, 23 to 79 A.D., used copper oxide with honey to treat intestinal worms. The Aztecs gargled with a mixture containing copper to treat sore throats. In a study carried out in a hospital, brass doorknobs showed sparse growth of pathogenic bacteria, while stainless steel doorknobs were heavily contaminated [2]. Previously published results [3, 4, 6-8, 10, 11 ,17 ,18] show that several bacterial species die on copper alloy surfaces in a matter of minutes to hours, and that Influenza A virus particles become inactivated on copper surfaces [9]. 

This paper discusses tests that were conducted on a range of commercial copper alloys. The tested organisms include _E. coli_ O157:H7, a food-borne pathogen associated with several large-scale food recalls, and Methicillin-resistant _Staphylococcus aureus_ (MRSA), a serious hospital-acquired, or nosocomial infection. According to a July 2004 report by the Infectious Disease Society of America, two million people are infected each year while in the hospital, and 70 % of these hospital-acquired or nosocomial infections are resistant to at least one drug. This results in 90,000 deaths in the U.S. annually. A March 2009 report by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) estimates the annual direct cost of Healthcare-Associated Infections in the U.S. to be $35-45 Billion [14]. 

In order to legally make antimicrobial public health claims in the United States, products must be approved and registered by the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). Antimicrobial claims fall under the Federal Insecticide Fungicide and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA). The EPA only requires efficacy testing when registrants wish to make public health claims. Some products, such as the commercially available silver ion-containing coatings, are registered under a special provision in FIFRA, the “treated article exemption” [15]. This provision indicates that the antimicrobial ingredient only protects the article containing the active ingredient. EPA grants the “treated article exemption” only for non-public health uses of a pesticide that is intended only to protect or preserve the treated article. One example of a “treated article exemption” is the addition of a fungicide to paint to prevent mildew. Thus, the fungicide is protecting the paint, and not public health. Therefore, products registered under the “treated article exemption” cannot legally make public health claims. Previously, only antimicrobial gases and liquids, such as sterilizers, disinfectants and sanitizers, could make public health claims under FIFRA. The results presented represent a summary of the required EPA-ap

proved efficacy tests. They were submitted along with the other required information, in pursuit of FIFRA registration. With five registrations granted on February 29, 2008, 275 antimicrobial copper alloys became the first solid materials legally permitted to make public health claims. The registrations were separated into five groups based on compositional ranges of nominal copper content. A sixth registration was granted on July 12, 2009 extending the number of registered alloys to 281, and reducing the allowable nominal copper content from 65 % to 60 %.

The chemical compositions of the copper alloys tested are listed in Table 1. As shown, they range from coppers to brasses and bronzes, copper-nickels and copper-nickel-zinc alloys (nickel silvers). The other materials tested include polyethylene, a common kitchen cutting board material, and a silver ion-containing coating which is being marketed as antimicrobial. The EPA public health registration of copper alloys is the first of several barriers to introducing antimicrobial copper alloys into hospitals and other healthcare applications. Alloy producers are now able to use data submitted to EPA by the Copper Development Association to obtain their own registrations required to sell products. Once federal registration is obtained, alloy producers must register with state EPA equivalents. To further assist copper alloy producers, the Copper Development

Association has obtained registrations in California, New York, and Florida, as these states have stricter data requirements. Once alloy producers register in the states, they can begin to market registered alloys with public health claims to customers and original equipment manufacturers. The applications with the highest likelihood of success are being identified, and the entire supply chain is being engaged. 

To fortify laboratory results, clinical trials are underway. Trials at three U.S. hospitals funded by the U.S. Department of Defense are testing the antimicrobial performance of copper alloys in a clinical setting. Items in Intensive Care Units (ICUs) were swabbed and cultured, and the most highly contaminated objects were identified [13]. These selected objects, including: I.V. poles, nurse’s call devices, patient tray tables, bedrails, visitor’s chairs and data input devices, were fabricated from antimicrobial copper alloys and installed in eight ICU rooms. The “copperized” components will be swabbed and compared to their non-copper equivalents in control rooms. Reduction of microbial surface contamination will be inspected, followed by the impact of copper surfaces on infection rates. 

Preliminary data from parallel trials taking place in Calama, Chile indicate an 85-100 % reduction in bacteria on the copper components compared to control objects. Similar trials in the U.K. also reported a 90-100 % reduction on the copper surfaces [1]. Clinical outcomes will be used to demonstrate antimicrobial performance in actual-use conditions. 

Copper alloy components are being fabricated and made readily available. Insight into the decisionmaking process in hospitals is being developed and better understood. It is necessary to gain acceptance among hospital administrators, infection control practitioners, government healthcare officials and the general public, as

well as architectural firms engaged in hospital construction. Widespread application of copper alloys should significantly decrease the number of viable bacteria found on human touch surfaces. The net result should be a reduction in nosocomial infections, the saving of lives, and a subsequent increase in copper alloy usage. Success will be attained when it is generally understood and appreciated that copper alloys should be utilized in those applications where their unique and intrinsic antimicrobial properties will benefit human health.

### Clinical Testing of Antimicrobial Copper Alloys 

Ph.D. Harold T. Michels, Adam A. Estelle, James H. Michel, Wilton R. Moran Copper Development Association, Inc. 260 Madison Avenue New York, NY 10016 

**Keywords:** Antimicrobial, copper alloys, hospital-acquired infection, infection control, surface disinfection 

#### Abstract 

Laboratory testing has demonstrated that a host of pathogenic organisms are killed or inhibited by copper surfaces. As a result, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency recently registered over 280 copper alloys as antimicrobial materials with public health claims. In order to demonstrate the benefit of copper touch surfaces in the clinical setting, trials at three Intensive Care Units (ICUs) are underway at the Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center (MSKCC) in New York City, the Medical University of South

Carolina (MUSC), and the Ralph H. Johnson VA Medical Center (RHJVA), both located in Charleston, South Carolina. The trials are funded by the U.S. Department of Defense under the Telemedicine and Advanced Technologies Research Center (TATRC). The trials examine environmental bacterial loads, infection rates, and impact on cross-contamination in ICU rooms retrofitted with copper touch surfaces in comparison to control rooms. Similar trials are also underway in the U. K., Germany, Chile, and Japan. 

#### 1 Introduction 

Healthcare Associated Infections (HAIs) are a growing concern that continue to challenge infection control programs throughout the world. Currently used hand and surface disinfection practices have fallen short, and opportunistic organisms that are ubiquitous in healthcare facilities continue to put patients and healthcare workers at risk. In the U.S. alone, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) estimate that HAIs cost U.S. Hospitals between 35 and 45 billion dollars annually [18]. It has also been reported that 80 % of infectious diseases are transmitted by touch [19], and typical pathogens found in healthcare facilities can survive on inanimate surfaces for days and even months [8]. Therefore, the inherent microbial burden of frequently touched surfaces in healthcare facilities may play a significant role in infection causality [2, 4, 6].

Copper alloys have emerged as a second line of defense against disease-causing organisms. Unprecedented registration with the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) permits this class of materials to make public health claims against five disease causing bacteria: _Staphylococcus aureus_ , MRSA (Methicillin-resistant _Staphylococcus aureus_ ), _Escherichia coli_ 0157:H7, _Enterobacter aerogenes_ and _Pseudomonas aeruginosa_ . Continually killing greater than 99.9 % of these five bacteria within two hours, copper alloys offer passive and ongoing protection in-between routine disinfection practices. EPA registration was granted based on extensive efficacy testing conducted under custom, Good Laboratory Practice (GLP) test protocols developed in conjunction with the EPA [1]. 

Although the antimicrobial properties of copper alloys have been demonstrated in the laboratory against a range of clinically important pathogens [1, 7, 9-15, 20-23], it is equally important to evaluate the performance of these materials in the clinical setting. In order to assess performance under actual use conditions, trials are underway at three Intensive Care Units (ICUs) at the Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center (MSKCC) in New York City, the Medical University of South Carolina (MUSC), and the Ralph H. Johnson VA Medical Center, both located in Charleston, South Carolina. The trials are funded by the U.S. Department of Defense under the Telemedicine and Advanced Technologies Research Center (TATRC). The trials examine e

nvironmental bacterial loads and rates of infection in ICU rooms retrofitted with copper touch surfaces in comparison to control rooms. Additional trials are underway at the Hospital de Calama in Chile, the Asklepios Klinik in Germany, and the Selly Oak Hospital in the United Kingdom. 

##### Disclaimer 

This paper includes conclusions about copper alloys that do not reflect U.S. EPA product registration approvals. These conclusions reflect the opinions of the researchers and authors. Any reference to effectiveness against other organisms has not been proven by U.S. EPA-approved testing. No claim of antimicrobial effectiveness is made, either express or implied, with regard to organisms other than those identified above. Further, any references that state or imply effectiveness in controlling disease or the transmission of bacteria that can cause disease in humans have not been approved by the U.S. EPA or FDA. Antimicrobial copper alloys cannot make “infectious disease control” claims. Copper alloy surface materials have been shown to reduce microbial contamination, but they do not necessarily prevent cross contamination.

#### 4 Asklepios Klinik, Hamburg, Germany

Over one million patients are treated in Asklepios hospitals each year. In an effort to quantify the impact of copper components in the clinical environment, Asklepios Klinik, identified several components to be replaced with copper equivalents and sampled for microbial contamination. ##### 5.2 Phase II: Microbial Burden Reduction Testing 

Once the copper components were installed, the trials entered Phase II in which copper and control surfaces were measured until ten weeks of data was obtained. For sampling, a template is placed over the participating object which is swabbed back and forth over the area to collect the resident microorganisms. Swabs were sent to the MUSC laboratory for processing where microbial counts per 100 cm<sup>2</sup> were produced and entered into a database. To better understand the impact of copper on clinical pathogens, several marker organisms were singled out to be analyzed including Methicillin-resistant _Staphylococcus aureus_ , Vancomycin-resistant _Enterococci_ , total _Staphylococci_ and gram-negative bacteria. The presence of these specific organisms on the components acts as an indicator of the inherent microbial burden of the room and ultimately the general risk level. This phase of the trials evaluates the ability of copper alloy surfaces to reduce the environmental microbial burden. While data collection for Phase II is still underway as of Fall 2009, preliminary data indicates a high reduction on the copper components compared to the controls on the order of 90 %. 

##### 5.3 Phase III: Impact on Infection Rate 

The final phase of the U.S. trials involves processing patient data to correlate the potential impact of copper components on infection rates. The trial hypotheses will test whether a lower inherent microbial burden reduces the relative risk of infection per patients’ time spent in the ICU. This will be the most difficult phase of the trials as infections are caused by a magnitude of factors that are difficult to identify and quantify. Additional analysis in Phase III will fingerprint organisms collected from the components and compare to organisms collected from patients to investigate the impact on cross-contamination. Phase III testing is scheduled to commence in Q2-Q3 of 2010. 

#### 6 Conclusions 

Extensive laboratory testing has provided a strong argument advocating the use of copper alloy surfaces to help combat microbial contamination in the healthcare environment. However, laboratory results do not necessarily reflect the performance of the materials in actual-use conditions which justifies the need for clinical evaluation. Several trials in various regions around the world have been conducted to investigate the clinical performance of antimicrobial copper alloy touch surfaces. Results obtained to date have demonstrated a high reduction (~90 %) of pathogenic microorganisms on copper alloy surfaces compared to non-

copper equivalents including plastic, stainless steel, and aluminium. The ongoing U. S. trials will add further validation to the existing trials by generating more statistically robust data as well as examining the impact on infection rates and crosscontamination. Clinical evidence has thus far supported laboratory work which suggests that copper alloys provide a second line of defense and should be utilized in those applications where their intrinsic antimicrobial properties will help kill human pathogens that cause infections.

#### Abstract 

The antimicrobial property of copper has been used for centuries but has never been fully quantified. This has changed in recent years with work coordinated by the Copper Development Association (US). Extensive laboratory testing resulted in U.S. Environmental Protection Agency registration of over 280 copper alloys as antimicrobial public health materials. 

The registration only covers five pathogens: _Staphylococcus aureus_ , MRSA (Methicillin-resistant _Staphylococcus aureus_ ), _Escherichia coli_ 0157:H7, _Enterobacter aerogenes_ and _Pseudomonas aeruginosa_ . However, other pathogens have also been tested on copper alloys including but not limited to: _Listeria monocytogenes_ , _Clostridium difficile_ , _Influenza_ A, _Acinetobacter baumanii_ , _Mycobacterium tuberculosis_ , _Candida albicans_ , _Klebsiella pneumoniae_ , _Legionella pneumonphila_ , Vancomycin-resistant _Enterococcus_ , _Salmonella enteric,_ and _Campylobacter jejuni_ . Copper has been shown to kill or inhibit the growth of all of these pathogens. 

This paper reviews the past antimicrobial efficacy testing on solid copper alloys and discusses results, potential applications, and future work. 

##### Disclaimer 

This paper includes conclusions about copper alloys that do not reflect EPA product registration approvals. These conclusions reflect the opinions of the researchers and authors. Any reference to effectiveness against other organisms has not been proven by U.S. EPA-approved testing. No claim of antimicrobial effectiveness is made, either express or implied, with regard to organisms other than those identified above. Further, any references that state or imply effectiveness in controlling disease or the transmission of bacteria that can cause disease in humans have not been approved by the U.S. EPA or FDA. Antimicrobial copper alloys cannot make “infectious disease control” claims.

#### 1 Introduction 

Healthcare Associated Infections (HAI) are a growing concern that continue to challenge infection control programs throughout the world. Currently instated hand and surface disinfection practices have fallen short, and opportunistic organisms that are ubiquitous in healthcare facilities continue to put patients and healthcare workers at risk. In the U.S. alone, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) estimate that HAIs cost U.S. Hospitals between 35 and 45 billion dollars annually [31]. It has also been reported that 80 % of infectious dise

ases are transmitted by touch [34]. Therefore, the inherent microbial burden of frequently touched surfaces in healthcare facilities may play a significant role in infection causality [3, 8, 9]. 

Copper alloys have emerged as a second line of defense against disease-causing organisms. Unprecedented registration with the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) permits this class of materials to make public health claims against five disease causing bacteria: _Staphylococcus aureus_ , MRSA (Methicillin-resistant _Staphylococcus aureus_ ), _Escherichia coli_ 0157:H7, _Enterobacter aerogenes_ and _Pseudomonas aeruginosa_ . Continually killing greater than 99.9 % of these five bacteria within two hours, copper alloys offer passive and ongoing protection in between routine disinfection practices [2]. EPA registration was granted based on extensive efficacy testing conducted under custom, Good Laboratory Practice (GLP) test protocols developed in conjunction with the EPA. 

In addition to the EPA registration, it is important to note that the efficacy of copper alloys against a range of important pathogens including viruses and fungi is well documented in the literature. A comprehensive review of the efficacy of solid copper alloys against a range of important organisms will be provided in order to gain perspective on the capabilities of these materials and justify enduse applications for copper in healthcare facilities and beyond. 

#### 2 Antimicrobial Efficacy Testing 

All tests were conducted at room temperature and ambient relative humidity to reflect actual use conditions unless indicated otherwise. Stainless steel alloy S30400 is typically used as the experimental control in efficacy tests as it has been recognized by the U.S. EPA to be biologically inert and exhibit no antimicrobial effect. 

Bacteria are omnipresent in healthcare facilities and continue to cause a great deal of healthcareassociated, or nosocomial, infections. _Staphylococci_ are ubiquitous bacteria that are easily transferred from patients to objects and healthcare workers. In fact, about 30 % of healthy persons are

##### 2.3 _Eschericia coli_ 0157:H7 

This bacterium is responsible for numerous food recalls, illnesses and deaths. Exposure can cause severe stomach cramps, vomiting and kidney failure. This strain of _E. coli_ is quite common and causes roughly 70,000 infections each year in the U. S. [5]. Numerous independent studies confirm that copper-based metals effectively kill this common bacterium [19, 27, 29, 33]. EPA registration permits over 280 copper-based metals to claim efficacy against _E. coli_ O157:H7. 

Early work by Dr. Phyllis Kuhn revealed that brass doorknobs in a hospital showed sparse bacterial growth while the stainless steel counterparts were heavily colonized. Kuhn conducted further experiments showing that little or no growth of _E. coli_ formed on copper and brass strips while heavy contamination occurred on aluminum and stainless steel samples [15]. 

More recent and controlled experiments by Noyce et al subjected various cast copper alloys to _E. coli_ . All alloys killed the organism in times ranging from 45 minutes to several hours (Figure 3) [27]. 

As mentioned before, Michels et al demonstrated that reducing the initial inoculation load expedites the kill time for copper challenged with MRSA [18]. Noyce et al also demonstrated this phenomenon with cast copper alloys challenged with _E. coli_ O157:H7 (Figure 4) [27]. 

Santo et al developed a different inoculation method to more accurately replicate actual use conditions. This work greatly reduced the time that the organism resides in a wet environment on the copper surface caused by the dilution process. This dry inoculation method actually expedited the kill time for 99 % pure copper (C11000) challenged with _E. coli_ O157:H7. Santo et al reported that copper samples killed over 10<sup>9</sup> CFUs in one minute at 23 °C [29]. At 5.5 °C, complete kill was achieved by C11000 in 4 minutes. Santo et al also tested a copper-nickel-zinc alloy (C75200, 65 % Cu) and a brass (C28000, max 62 % Cu). Both alloys killed over 10<sup>9</sup> CFUs of _E. coli_ within 15 min [29].

##### 2.4 _Clostridium difficile_ 

This spore forming bacterium is highly resilient and occurs most often in patients taking antibiotics. Kramer et al reported that _Clostridium difficile_ ( _C. diff_ ) spores can survive on dry, inanimate surfaces for up to five months [13]. 

Due to the resilient nature of this bacterium, copper alloys take longer to kill the spores of this pathogen compared to other tested organisms. Weaver et al demonstrated that five copper alloys ranging from 65 % to 100 % copper content killed greater than 10<sup>5</sup> CFUs of _C. diff_ spores between 24 and 48 hours (see Figure 5) [35]. 

Although 24 hours may seem like too long of a response, efficacy demonstrated by copper alloys is quite meaningful considering _C. diff_ spores can survive for months on other inanimate surfaces [13]. 

Separate testing conducted by Wheeldon et al utilized a germinant to enhance copper’s efficacy against _C. diff_ spores [35]. A germinant is a chemical often found in standard hospital disinfectants that induces spore formation in microorganisms. _C. diff_ can cycle between vegetative and germination states to prolong survival. This “germination theory” suggests that _C. diff_ spores are more susceptible to copper in the germination state. By inducing the spore-forming state, Wheeldon et al reported a > 99 % reduction of over 10<sup>6</sup> CFUs/cm<sup>2</sup> in three hours on pure copper [36]. This study suggests that germinants, often found in standard hospital disinfectants, may enhance the antimicrobial efficacy of copper alloys against _Clostridium difficile_ spores.

#### Abstract 

Copper tubes + copper strips are the preferred materials in heat exchange elements at solar collectors of flatpanel absorbers and vacuum tube absorbers. Solar collector absor

bers made of copper have the best performance and also completely positive results in usage after a longterm experience over more than 20 years. Key requests are to produce the copper semis with excellent quality and at the same time at acceptable cost. Also a concept with an efficient transport logistic is important as an optimised link between copper semi producers and solar thermal absorber producers. 

#### 1 Copper strips and copper tubes as pre-materials 

The comfortable use of sunbeam thermal heat capacity for building heating and to keep warmwater for bathroom and kitchen – this is an always-lasting desire of humans. We are beginning now to accustom us to the fact that this desire was converted already for some time into commercial and proven technology. In the meantime in a lot of countries – including Germany – solarthermal solutions belong to the advanced everyday life. Only since approx. 25-30 years the existing substantial technical level of development made it possible that since then thermal solar use was large-scale introduced as the normal state of the art in the supply of warming. Today solar thermal uses are well-accepted and confirmed as modern, ecologically favourable, payable, safe and longlived. 

In result the installed solar thermal capacity and its continuously growing rate in Europe now is at an impressive high level (Figure 1). The 12 countries which are dominating the European installation and production of solarthermic equipment are presented in (Figure 2).

Well known are the solar absorbers mainly at roofs of buildings (Figure 3) but possible, too, at walls. Main priority is the right position to the sun (right angle to the horizon, long time of sun exposition) to collect a daily maximum of solar heat. The solar heat uses the physical condition that the sun-emitted beams are containing a mixture of light energy and thermal energy. If sunbeams meet solid surfaces, a part of the thermal energy (together with heat caused by converted photons) is absorbed by this surface and conducted into the body below. The remaining parts of the sunbeams are reflected, and are not any longer available for the thermal solar use. 

The once heated surface of solar energy absorbers is designed to transmit the warmth by lowest energy losses into a liquid circulation of a tubular system. This transports the warmth to the need place (room heater, water heater), and to the heat accumulator in case of missing need. The inadvertent calorific losses are possible at many places and must be limited by isolation to a minimum.

**Keywords:** Copper infiltration, Tungsten skeleton, W/Cu compacts 

#### Abstract 

Elements with high heat conductivity are infiltrated into tungsten porous skeletons to fabricate high performance heat sinks. Copper and silver are two popular infiltrants. Copper is more popular since it costs less than silver. In this research, a Tungsten porous skeleton was prepared with cold isostatic pressing and subsequently sintered at 1800 °C under a protective atmosphere. 12 wt. % Cu was infiltrated into porous skeleton by directional infiltration. Previous related works on the infiltration of copper were focused on at least 15 wt. % Cu. For this new condition, copper was infiltrated at different conditions to investigate the effects of process parameters. 1300 °C and 60 min were found to be the optimum infiltration temperature and time for a nearly completed process. 

#### 1 Introduction 

Tungsten/copper compacts are widely used in materials, mechanical and electrical engineering. Resistance welding electrodes, electrical discharge machine, and heat sinks are some of their common applications. Tungsten has a high thermal conductivity, the highest melting point amongst the metals, and a suitable dimentional stability at high temperature. Copper is well-known for having the highest thermal conductivity after silver among the metals. So a microstructure that contains W and Cu is very appropirate for heat sink applications in high temperature environments [1]. 

W/Cu compacts are commonly fabricated by two methods: hot pressing [2] and copper infiltration into tungsten porous skeleton [3, 4]. In the hot pressing method, tungsten and copper powders are first mixed to obtain a homogeneous mixture. The mixture is poured into a graphite die. Then it is pressed at a high temperature which leads to a simultaneous pressing and sintering. Although the hot pressing method is faster and can produce near net shape parts, because of technological limitations, it is not applicable for large products. On the other hand, in the infiltration method, a Tugsten porous skeleton is prepared and placed in the vicinity of molten Cu so that Cu will fill the porosities 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

247 

_Samei, Alvani, Green, Stoilov_ 



by the action of capillary forces. The driving force of this procedure is the decrease in surface free energy. Loss of solubility of copper in tungsten makes suitable infiltration conditions. Since copper is very sensitive to oxygen at high tempertures, the infiltration process is perfomed in a hydrogen protective atmosphere. Hydrogen is also found to be the most effective atmosphere for improvement of tungsten powder sintering [5]. 

Infiltration of ≥ 15 wt. % Cu in tungsten skeletons has been studied in detail before. However, when the amount of infiltrant is decreased, the skeleton prosity percentage should be normally decreased. So closed porosities that can not be filled by the infiltrant may appear.

Also the mean size of the porosities changes which affects the infiltration process. In this research, the effects of the processing temperature and the time of infiltration of 12 wt. % Cu into the tungsten skeleton were studied and the optimized condition is reported. 

#### 2 Experimental procedure 

##### 2.1 Tungsten skeleton 

Tungsten and copper densities are 19.3 and 8.96 g/cm<sup>3</sup> , respectively, and 12 wt. % of copper was supposed to be infiltrated, so the goal was to obtain sintered skeletons with 25.85 vol. % porosity [12 Ч (193. / .896) ≅ 25.85]. In other words W- 25.85 vol. % Cu is equivalent to W-12 wt. % Cu. 

Tungsten powder with 99.9 % purity and an average particle size of 5.4 µm was used to prepare the skeleton. The powder was poured into plastic molds (Φ2.0Ч10.0 cm) for cold isostatic pressing (CIP). After a trial and error procedure, the ultimate pressure was found to be 200 MPa during the CIP process. Green skeletons were sintered under an argon + 20 % hydrogen protective atmosphere at 1800 °C for 60 min. The final skeleton densities were determined using MPIF #42 standard that were 73.7-74.5 % of theoretical density. In other words, there was 25.5-26.3 % that was acceptable. The sintered tungsten rods were cut into Φ1.5Ч1.8 cm parts for the infiltration process. 

##### 2.2 Copper directional infiltration processing 

A graphite die (Figure 1) was used for the infiltration process. This die was designed to obtain several samples in each infiltration process for various tests. The geometry of each die is shown in Figure 2. High purity (99.99 %) copper wire was cut and placed in the bottom of each die. The tungsten skeleton located above the copper. In this way, the upward directional infiltration condition was prepared. The amount of copper in each die was 3 times more than the needed amount. The infiltration was performed at 1200, 1250, 1300 and 1350 °C for 30, 60 and 90 min at the maximum temperature. The heating and cooling rates were 10 °C/s. A hydrogen protective atmosphere was used.

However, at 60 and 90 min, temperature increment is effective up to 1300 °C and increasing the temperature to 1350 °C is just a waste of energy. According to Hagen-Poiseuille [6] the kinetics of infiltration phenomena highly depends on the time and on the viscosity of the fluid, i.e. the molten copper. e infiltration process at 1300 °C for 60 min, and according to Table 1, the final relative density of 98.0 % will be obtained. Since no tangible improvement occurs by infiltrating at 1350 °C for 90 min, it can be said that the infiltration process is approximately completed at 1300 °C after 60 min and that the ~2 % difference with the theoretical density is related to closed pores in tungsten skeleton that cannot be filled by the molten copper.

#### 4 Conclusion 

In this research, a W-12 wt. % Cu compact was produced using the directional infiltration method. For this purpose, tungsten porous skeletons with 73.7-74.5 % of the theoritical density were prepared using powder metallurgy processes. The infiltration process was perfomed at four different temperatures with three various durations. Results show that a nearly complete infiltration is obtainable at 1300 °C for 60 min under a Hydrogen protective atmosphere. The final microstructure includes a continuous copper net that is a rapid path of heat conduction and is effective for heat sink applications.

### Structure and Properties of Copper Ecological Alloys Designed for Elements of Fittings 

Prof. Dr. Inż. Z. Śmieszek, Doc. Dr. Inż. L. Ciura, Mgr. Inż. B. Cwolek, Mgr. Inż. W. Malec, Dr. Inż. B. Juszczyk, Mgr Inż. Ł. Wierzbicki (Marchewka) 

Institute of Non Ferrous Metals Sowińskiego 5 Gliwice, Poland 

**Keywords:** Lead free brass, bismuth, bronze, microstructure, castability, mechanical properties 

#### Abstract 

The study presents results of investigations into a group of environmentally friendly copper alloys used mainly in production of components of fittings. The objective of the study was to evaluate possibilities for partial or complete elimination of harmful lead in the brasses used in fittings by replacing it with other eco-friendly elements. The study covered three groups of alloys: 

- of limited lead content, 

- of limited lead content and small bismuth content, 

- of complete lead elimination. 

It was assumed that the newly developed alloys should present a comparable level of technological properties and usability to the currently used brasses. For comparison, one of the most popular lead brasses was used of the grade CB753S (MO59 according to the Polish Standard PN-92/H-87025). 

The alloys were produced in laboratory conditions by melting in induction furnace of open crucible of capacity 50 kg of Cu. The produced alloys were subjected to the investigations into influence of chemical composition and melting and casting conditions on their structure and properties. The structure was evaluated by optic microscope and scanning electron microscope (SEM). Uniformity of chemical composition in microregions was also evaluated, by EDS method. Mechanical properties (Rm, Rp0.2, A, Z) were determined by axial tension tests conducted in room temperature, while the casting properties (castability, shrinkage) basing on the spiral test casting and measurements of changes in geometrical parameters of the casts. Within the scope of technological properties examination, a test of machinability at variable machine cutting rates was conducted, and the produced chips were examined and evaluated. 

Considering the interesting results reached for the bismuth containing alloys, also detailed analysis of the influence of such alloy additions as: tin, aluminium, iron, phosphorus, boron and nickel on

their technological and mechanical properties was performed. The studies were conducted mainly for improvement of mechanical and casting properties of the newly developed alloys. 

The obtained results of the investigations were verified in pilot scale in cooperation and under supervision of the industrial partner – one of the le

ading Polish manufacturer of fittings – Armatura Krakow S.A. A batch of selected components of fittings way of production, which was then subjected to mechanical working, then grinding and polishing, and galvanic treatment. The quality assessment, as used in that Company, was applied on thus prepared samples. The results confirmed the assumptions and usability of the newly developed, eco-friendly alloys for production of components of the fittings. 

#### 1 Introduction 

Strong emphasis placed recently on taking ecological measures results in limitations or complete elimination of some harmful substances, including lead, from industrial practice. The copper alloys which are widely used for components of fittings max. contain about 3.5 % of that element. 

Further limitations with respect to purity of drinking water brought restrictive quality requirements and turned attention to the components of installations which are made of lead containing copper alloys. In the result US Congress introduced changes into the legislation on drinking water (so called _Safe Drinking Water Act_ – SWDA), which limited application of the materials used for components of water systems. 

The described above limitations have significant importance not only for American industry but also on European manufacturers of casting alloys and producers of fittings. It is a consequence of intensive trading with the USA and of increasingly common practice of adoption of current standards by EU countries. Since January 1, 2006 the EU Directive 98/83/EC [1] limited the allowed lead content in the drinking water to 25 µg/l. According to the Directive the permitted level of selenium and copper content is 10 µg/l and 2 mg/l, respectively. The Directive provides also for further limitations to be enforced in 2013 for lead content not to exceed 10 µg/l. The provision were implemented in Poland within the scope of the Law on collective water supply and collective carrying out of sewage [2]. 

Limitation of the lead which passes to the water during installation operation is only one of the obstacles in using lead containing alloys. Strong emission of lead vapour during its melting and casting is another problem, as well as the waste generated, e.g. in a form of moulding mass. In the future also all lead containing scrap can cause difficulties if qualified as harmful waste and subjected to strict rules for dumping and processing. 

The presented above legal and technological conditions resulted in intensive research conducted by the USA and other countries into limitation of lead content in components of fittings or develop-

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_

ment of new materials which can serve the same purpose but without lead addition. The problem can be solved in the following ways: 

- by development of copper alloys in which lead will be substituted with addition of other element of si

milar influence on the alloy, 

- by significant reduction of lead content to the permissible level at the same time introducing some modifying additions, 

- by development of other casting copper alloys which can substitute the currently used ones. 

A preliminary analysis has shown that bismuth can be seen as a potential lead substitute. Previous studies covered also other elements, such as: sulphur, selenium and tellurium [3-6], which mainly influence machining properties of the alloys. 

The conducted in many world research centers studies into possibilities of substituting lead with bismuth contributed to the development of commercial casting copper alloys which, according to the modifying additions used, can be divided into: 

- Bi + P, In, Sn additions 

- Bi + mischmetal 

- Bi + Se. 

The group of lead-free copper alloys with addition of bismuth and modifying addition of mischmetal was developed and patented in the USA by Singh [7-10], and then commercialized by Federal Metal Company USA under the trade name _Federalloy_ . The group is composed of about 15 alloys, both bronzes and brasses. Proper mechanical and machining properties in those alloys were reached by addition of bismuth and mischmetal as a modifier or by admixture of rare earth metals. 

Another group of materials is composed of copper alloys in which addition of bismuth and selenium was used simultaneously. They found their commercial applications in a form of a group of alloys initially called _SeBiLoy_ , and currently known under the trade name _EnviroBrass_ . Good machining properties of those alloys results from presence of Bi and Se, since their combined presence has stronger effect on the alloy than each of the elements separately [11, 12]. Additionally, bismuth hampers washing selenium out of the alloy, which has special influence on drinking water quality. The experience gathered in that area was also used in development of other casting alloys of that group [13, 14]. 

Complete elimination of lead-containing alloys and introduction of lead-free alloys in their place would result in necessity to use lead-free scrap for their production. Because of the huge market of lead-containing brasses and other lead-containing alloys the existing supply of the scrap which contains lead is very high and it can be expected that for a long time it will dominate secondary materials market. The complete ban on lead-containing copper alloys would make utilization of that scrap impossible. That would also result in necessity for its metallurgical treatment for Pb removal which, in turn, would entail high costs. 

Another important aspect of introduction of lead-free alloys is significantly higher price of final products resulting from utilization of more expensive types of scrap (lead-free) and significantly 

257 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

_Śmieszek, Ciura, Cwolek, Malec, Juszczyk, Wierzbicki (Marchewka)_ 



more expensive alloy additions. Growing demand for bismuth should al

so cause further increase in price of that metal. 

A certain solution can be seen in removal of lead from surfaces having contact with water. Results of the studies, in which good solubility of lead in acetate solution was used, conducted to determine possibilities for removal of lead from surfaces after machining [15] showed high efficiency of such chemical treatment of the products. There are developed technologies in the area of chemical surface treatment for Pb removal (e.g. so called Kunkel process [16, 17] used by manufacturer of waterworks products Ford Meter Box Company, Inc) which, as shown in the published test results [18], are successfully used in production. 

The second similar research direction covers alloys which contain small lead addition, too small to ensure the required functional characteristics, and some amount of bismuth (with possible selenium addition as well). Combination of those two elements ensures good properties of the casts, at the same time providing possibilities for utilisation of lead containing scrap. It can be applied, of course, to the brasses and to bronzes of wide range of applications, e.g. for components of fittings and for slide bearings. 

The mentioned above conditions will have a fundamental influence on the future administrative and technological solutions which will be binding also in the EU. Therefore, there is a strong need to conduct research into creation of new materials of properties which are adjusted to specific needs – taking under consideration not only their functional characteristics for specific conditions of production process but also potential requirements with respect to Pb content and pollution of environment. 

The objective of the research conducted in this study was to determine influence of selected alloy additions on technological and functional properties and structure of examined group of alloys. 

#### 2 Criteria for selection of lead substitute 

The following criteria were accepted in selection of potential lead substitute in the alloys: 

- toxicity, 

- economic aspects, 

- physicochemical properties. 

The results of the analysis conducted with respect to properties, costs, produced volumes and relative toxicity of possible lead substitutes has shown that in practice only bismuth can be taken under consideration `.`

#### 5 Conclusions 

1. The conducted studies led to development of new environmentally friendly copper alloys. The produced alloys, both without lead and with limited content of that element, present properties comparable to the currently used alloys of MO59 and B555 type. 

2. It was established that addition of bismuth in the amount of 1% results in the best mechanical and casting properties of the brasses. In the case of bronzes the highest casting properties were reached in the alloys which contain silicon and manganese, however at the same time mechanical properties were reduced. Addition of iron and aluminium at the level of 1% results in improvement of mechanical properties. The additional effect of introduction of those elements was elimination of porosity in the bronzes. 

3. Pilot tests showed that the produced brasses present good castability and machining properties. Additionally, in the case of lead-free alloy with bismuth addition the casting temperature was significantly lower than in popular alloy (CB753S), which may bring significant reduction of production costs in the future. 

4. The conducted industrial tests confirmed usability of the newly developed alloys for electroplating. The produced alloys show good machining properties and have smooth surface after machine cutting.

### Practical Examples for the Reduction of Energy Consumption in a Copper Rod Mill 

Dr. A. Wilbrand, Dr. S. Schneider 

Deutsche Giessdraht GmbH KupferstraЯe 5 Emmerich, Germany 

**Keywords:** Copper, wire rod, rod mill, energy efficiency, waste gas, cooling water, compressed air 

#### Abstract 

Energy consumption has to be considered as one of the key performance indicators of copper wire rod plants. Today the economic usage of energy is a must in respect to cost effects and environmental aspects. Against the background of limited availability of fossil fuel and various obstacles to the setup of new energy supply infrastructures in many countries the saving of energy is of crucial importance for energy-intensive industries. 

In a copper wire rod plant natural gas is the main energy source for melting the copper cathodes and keeping the molten copper at casting temperatures. Electrical energy is mainly used for the rolling mill, the various pumps for the liquid media, the blowers that provide the combustion air for the natural gas burners and, finally, for the generation of compressed air. Continuous improvement of the efficiency of the use of

energy has a permanent effect on the specific consumption of natural gas and electric power. 

Examples of technical measures will be presented that have greatly reduced energy consumption at Deutsche Giessdraht GmbH in Emmerich, Germany. Among these are the following: a) a heat exchanger that feeds abundant waste gas energy into the facility’s heating and sanitary water systems, b) a cooling appliance that uses scrap rod to prevent superheating of the molten copper, c) coolingwater pumps with variable pumping rates that operate at a reduced pressure level, d) a special technology that allows a reduced use of compressed air in the rod treatment line. 

#### 1 Introduction 

The forthcoming scenario of energy supply can be characterized as follows: The next decades are expected to be affected by an increasing tightness of crude oil and a changing supply scenario for natural gas. The usage of energy which is based on fossil fuel has an impact on carbon dioxide

emissions and thereby also on the future development of the global climate. The construction and installation of new electrical power plants in Germany and other European countries is going to be hindered by a multitude of socio-political influences irrespective of whether nuclear energy, coal or natural gas are used as the primary energy source. For various reasons the implementation of regenerative technologies for power generation still is far from becoming the supporting leg of the energy supply infrastructure. 

Already today this scenario has led to a strong increase of energy prices, so that energy consumption, which after labour costs is the largest cost factor for a copper wire rod plant like Deutsche Giessdraht GmbH, increasingly affects the production cash costs. With regard to business-level economy for a rod mill as a part of the energy-intensive industry saving of energy is of utter importance. At the same time this corresponds with the political will to reduce dependence on energy supply and carbon dioxide emissions. 

In a copper wire rod plant natural gas is the main energy source for melting the copper cathodes and keeping the molten copper at casting temperatures during transfer to the casting machine via slag pots, holding furnace, tundish and the launders in-between these aggregates. Electrical energy is mainly used for the rolling mill, the various pumps for the liquid media, the blowers that provide the combustion air for the natural gas burners and, finally, for the generation of compressed air. Continuous improvement of the efficiency of the use of energy has a permanent effect on the specific consumption of natural gas and electric power. 

#### 2 Improvements of energy efficiency 

During the investigation of the current status of energy efficiency at Deutsche Giessdraht several fields for possible improvements were identified. Among these were: recovery of abundant waste gas energy, optimization of th

e feed of scrap rod back into the process, modernization of coolingwater pumps and replacement of compressed air used for rod drying purposes by an alternative technique. In the following the solutions implemented to enhance the energy efficiency in these fields are described in detail covering applications in the melting area, the area where the molten copper is transferred from the melting furnace to the casting machine, the casting, rolling and pickling area and the area of the rod inspection line. 

##### 2.1 Waste gas heat exchanger 

The process of wire rod production starts with the melting of copper cathodes in a shaft furnace fired with natural gas. Technical solutions for recovery of abundant energy from the waste gas leaving the cathode shaft furnace depend on the temperature level and the cleanness level of the waste gas and have to be integrated into the concept for removal of the dust contained in the waste gas. The shaft furnace at Deutsche Giessdraht is equipped with a bag filter that allows a maximum gas

The payback period is estimated to 4 years. The heat exchanger was installed in late December 2007.
