to relay information about the proposed mine to the community and to solicit meaningful input from the local stakeholders. While not a complete success, Kennecott’s CSR approach has worked well enough to keep the permitting process online and moving forward. 

#### 6 Discussion 

The evolving permitting laws in Wisconsin and Michigan have created more involvement of the public in the decision-making process. This change has led to opposing stakeholders becoming more sophisticated in their ability to communicate their message to other stakeholders and put political pressure on government decision-makers. Mining companies have responded by communicating their views to the other stakeholders as well. The result has been competing dialogues between the mining companies and those in opposition to the mine as they try to reach the other stakeholders (local residents and government officials). The competing dialogues center on three basic questions: What is the best economic direction for the local community? Can technology and its application adequately protect the environment? Do mining companies (and government) have the same values as the local community about the environment and sustainability? 

With the Eagle Project, Kennecott adopted a CSR approach and formed a Community Advisory Group in order to be accepted by the stakeholders in the local community. Kennecott made CSR a distinctive theme, and it appears to have achieved mixed results. Kennecott’s CAG is an effort to be inclusive and give local groups an opportunity to be directly informed about Kennecott’s plans and to provide feedback. Kennecott believes it got the majority of the community behind the proposal for the mine through its CAG and the permitting process has been successful to date. However the main opponents of the mine were not persuaded to change their views and they continued their competing dialogues. Presently, they have gone to court to try overturn the permits. This same pattern was seen at the Wisconsin sites a

s well. 

Why has Kennecott’s effort not worked with some of the stakeholder groups [1]? If the role of CSR is to create solutions that meet the goals of both the mining company and the local community, then CSR requires addressing all the issues raised by stakeholders. In the Eagle Project, Kennecott’s strong belief in its science and technology may have prevented it from understanding the level of concern about environmental risk in stakeholder discourses. Kennecott may have interpreted their concern as a failure to understand the science and technology that would mitigate risk instead of uncertainty about the ability of the science and technology to deliver as promised. These misunderstandings could make meaningful dialogue across stakeholder discourse communities leading to collaborative solutions more difficult. This can have the unintended consequence of raising the emotional level of the discourse against mining and escalating conflict. 

Although CSR is by definition the strategy of a firm, stakeholders also have something to learn about engaging in discourse with a CSR firm. If stakeholders define community too narrowly by defending primarily the interests aligned with their social purposes at the exclusion of all others, 

361 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

_Campbell, Walck, Hartingh_ 



they may also hinder or preclude the possibility of interacting with a firm and its other stakeholders to craft a solution. If stakeholders fail to listen effectively to the beliefs and values of the mining companies and their supporters and use emotional, divisive language, they risk being judged prematurely and closing communication channels. 

It is of course quite possible that the conflicting social purposes of multiple discourse communities cannot be resolved through a strategy of CSR which seeks to meet both the goals of the mining company and the goals of society, by voluntarily finding mutually-acceptable solutions that allow mining while reducing risk through responsible practices. If the risks of a proposed mine are deemed too high, and trust in the mining company is low, opposing stakeholder groups may simply adopt a conflict-generating and legal strategy to stop a mine or to win significant concessions in the way a mine is implemented. This has clearly happened in the cause of the Eagle Project. In that case, a CSR strategy will have little effect on those stakeholders, and the mining company needs to implement a strategy of mediation and conflict resolution. The success of the permitting process is determined by how many of the stakeholders are open to the CSR strategy of the mining company and how many are not. For the Crandon Project there were too many in the former group and for the Eagle Project less. 

#### 7 Conclusion 

As learned from the case studies, a mining company wishing to get a new mine permitted must not only meet the legal and technical requirements established by the state but must also hold its own in the communicat

ion of views to the public. Mining companies like Kennecott have moved toward CSR and its themes as a way to gain public support for their proposals and to counter the barrage of public criticisms from opposed stakeholders. The use of CSR apparently has little effect with stakeholders whose views and philosophies are so divergent from those of the mining company that there is no common ground for discussion and compromise. Accordingly, the success or failure of a permitting effort depends to some extent to the size and influence of such stakeholder groups. This difference is seen with the Crandon case with the large and significant involvement of Native American communities as compared to the Flambeau Mine and Eagle project where more of the stakeholders were open to discussion and compromise. The mining company’s success depends on its ability to persuade enough stakeholders to accept its message of CSR instead of the anti-mining message of the opposing stakeholders. The use of CSR and stakeholder engagement can help do this if stakeholders are willing to listen and accept what is said. If the company can’t do this, they could well face the situation like Crandon where many stakeholder groups were persuaded to accept the anti-mining message of the opposing groups.

### The EU Copper Risk Assessment: Summary and Applications 

K. Delbeke et al. 

European Copper Institute Brussels, Tervurenlaan 168, B-1050 Brussels, Belgium, 

All co-authors and related addresses are listed in the section co-authors 

**Keywords:** Copper, risk assessment, EU regulations 

#### Abstract 

The copper risk assessment report concludes that copper uses are generally safe to man and the environment. Contemporary occupational exposure to copper, and its resultant systemic absorption, is generally low in plants operating to current best practice and is not predicted to result in adverse health effects. Some remaining data gaps (marine effects and effects from inhalation exposure) and some local aquatic site risks were identified and are being addressed. 

The risk assessment was initiated by the copper industry, anticipating existing and upcoming EU regulations such as REACH (EC/1907/2006) and the Water Framework Directive (2000/60/EC). The EU Technical Committee on New and Existing Substances (TCNES) and the EU Scientific Committee on Health and Environmental risks (SCHER) have reviewed the reports and support the results and conclusions drawn. 

The methodologies developed in co-operation with other stakeholders (e.g. Eurometaux, other metal associations) and the results from the copper risk assessment report have obtained recognition in other EU regulatory frameworks. The copper risk assessment is currently being considered under the Biocidal Products Directive (BPD), REACH and the Water Framework Directive. Further acceptance of the novel approaches and models on the incorporation of bioavailability are needed and critical to future assessments of metal concentrations in the various EU regulatory frameworks. 

#### 1 Introduction 

Anticipating existing and upcoming EU regulations such as REACH (EC/1907/2006) and Water Framework Directive (WFD) (2000/60/EC), the copper industry initiated in 2000 a comprehensive Voluntary Risk Assessment (VRA) of copper and several copper compounds. The assessment process was developed in co-operation with the Italian Government’s Istituto Superiore di Sanitа, acting 

365 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

_Delbeke et al._ 



as the review country on behalf of the European Commission and the EU Member States. In May 2005, on behalf of the European Copper Institute, Italy submitted the draft risk assessment for review by the European Commission and the EU Member States. The reviews from the EU Technical Committees on New and Existing Substances (TCNES) and from the EU Scientific Committee on Health and Environmental risks (SCHER) were finalized in 2009. For the BPD and REACH, the European Chemicals Bureau (ECB) and the European

Chemicals agency (ECHA), agreed on harmonisation with the copper risk assessment report. 

This paper provides an overview of the main conclusions drawn from the 1800-page dossier and assesses how the results and conclusions can be used across some critical EU regulations. 

#### 2 Methodology used for the copper Risk Assessment 

The EU copper risk assessment, evaluated the emissions into the EU-15 from production, use and disposal of copper and four copper compounds (copper(I)oxide, copper(II)oxide, copper oxychloride, copper(II)sulphate pentahydrate). The assessment was performed in accordance to the EU Regulation 793/93 and followed the principles laid down in the EU RA EU Technical Guidance Document [1]. 

A comprehensive assessment of the health and environmental effects from copper exposures during copper production, use, recycling, and disposal was performed. Information from the producers of anodes, cathodes, copper powders and copper chemicals, as well as from many semi-fabricators, cable companies and other downstream users, was collected from over 100 sites across the EU. Copper levels in air, food, drinking water were compared against human safe threshold values. Copper levels in surface waters, sediments, soils and sewage treatment plants were compared against the appropriate predicted no-effect concentrations (PNECS). 

As metal characteristics are not appropriately considered in the EU Technical Guidance Document [1], metal-specific guidelines were developed by a metals industry initiative, led by Eurometaux (the non ferrous metals’ industry representative body), and supported by the European Commission and several EU Member States [2, 3]. For copper, the relevant risk assessment characteristics included in the assessment are: 

1. Copper is naturally occurring, with background levels varying with the local geology. These have been considered when evaluating copper exposure levels; 

2. Copper is an essential nutrient for all life forms and therefore, human health and environmental limits have been based on a scientific evaluation of the potential risks with regard to both deficiency and excess; 

3. Copper ions entering the environment through natural or anthropogenic (man-made) processes (also “routes”), are naturally detoxified in the mineral cycle. Indeed, the binding of copper ions to natural, dissolved and particulate organic matter in water, sediment and soils reduces their bioavailability. On the other hand, chelation of ions makes Cu available to plant nutrition and binding to dissolved organic matter can result in copper transport from soils and in aqueous environments.

#### 3 Key results and conclusions from the copper risk assessment 

##### 3.1 Human health risk characterisation 

Under the EU risk assessment framework, potential hazards, associated with copper exposures were evaluated and risks to the general populati

on and the workers assessed by comparing typical and reasonable worst case (RWC) exposures to the safe threshold values. The EU risk assessment framework is driven by anthropogenic substances and thus, only risks for excess are normally assessed. Copper is however an essential element and in the copper risk assessment report, an additional assessment was made of risks from deficiency for the general population. 

The results and conclusions were already summarised in [4]. The results have now been endorsed by TCNES and SCHER and posted on the ECHA website [5]. The main conclusions can be summarized as: 

- **Copper is well regulated.** The concentration of copper in the body is strictly and efficiently regulated by homeostatic mechanisms. Systemic effects occur when the capacity of the homeostasis is exceeded. The major control mechanism is gastrointestinal absorption and biliary excretion into faeces. Homeostatic control mechanisms lead to copper absorption from the gastrointestinal tract, decreasing with increasing dose. For humans, the observed range in oral copper absorption was 60-30 %. As an example, an oral intake of 1 mg Cu/day results in systemic absorption of 60 %, an intake of 2 mg Cu/day results in systemic absorption of 55 %, an intake of 8 mg Cu/day results in systemic absorption of 30 %. 

The failure to maintain homeostasis may lead to adverse effects resulting either from deficiency or excess. Copper deficiency is more frequent and causes far more severe adverse health effects than copper toxicity. 

- **Copper deficiency may be of concern in Europe.** No conclusive Deficiency Effect Level (DEL) was derived but dietary intake of 1 mg Cu/day has been shown to be sufficient to maintain the copper balance. An extensive literature review of the actual dietary copper intakes of the European citizens demonstrated daily copper intake ranges between 0.6 and 2 mg, suggesting that deficiency may be of concern. 

- **Copper exposures are generally safe** . Animal and human studies show that repeated elevated oral copper intakes affect the liver. An internal systemic safe threshold value of 0.041 mg/kg body weight/day was derived from animal data and due consideration of dose-dependent copper absorption from the gastrointestinal tract (see above). For a person of 70 kg this would correspond to an upper limit of 11.4 mg/person/day for ingested copper. 

   - Actual daily oral intakes through diet and drinking water, range between 0.6 and 2 mg Cu/day. Dermal exposure (e.g. handling of coins) is negligible due to very low dermal adsorption of copper, ranging between 0.03 % (dry particles) to 0.3 % (wet particles). Inhalation exposures are generally very small and hardly contribute to the overall copper intake of the European citizens. 

367 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

_Delbeke et al._ 



The data from the combined exposures demonstrate that there is no concern of long term health effects for the general population. 

Acute nausea and othe

r gastrointestinal irritation effects, associated with copper in drinking water was assessed and allowed to derive an external safe threshold value of 4 mg/l. The reasonable worst case exposure value of 2.11 mg Cu/liter for acute drinking water intake is below the threshold value and suggests no risks of acute toxicity. Potential effects need to be considered in rare cases, characterized by “corrosive” drinking water (high copper concentration). 

- **The industrial measures that are in place do protect workers** . Inhalation exposures vary depending on the tasks of the workers. Few data are available on inhalation absorption. For estimating absorption via inhalation, based on particle size distribution the deposition in different parts of the respiratory tract was modeled. For the pulmonary fraction 100 % was assumed, for the other fractions the value for absorption in the gastrointestinal tract was taken. For dermal absorption, 0.3-0.03 % was taken. Workers exposures were compared to the systemic safe threshold value (0.041 mg/kg body weight/day), with due consideration of the different exposure routes and appropriate absorption factors. 

Contemporary occupational exposure to copper, and its resultant systemic absorption, is generally low in plants operating to current best practice and is not predicted to result in adverse health effects. During the production of copper cathodes, semis and cables no risks are anticipated when normal industrial recommended risk management measures are respected. For the production of copper powders some risks were anticipated in cases where respiratory equipment was not used. 

- **Copper is not a substance of high concern.** Based on an extensive literature review, copper and copper compounds evaluated in the copper voluntary risk assessment are considered not to be Carcinogenic, Mutagenic and not to have effects on Reproduction (CMR). 

- **Data-gap analysis:** The TCNES and authorities involved in the Biocidal products directive expressed concern related to the absence of adequate data on inhalation toxicity. An additional study is now on the way. 

##### 3.2 Environmental risk characterisation 

Under the EU risk assessment framework, the highest concentrations that demonstrate no-effects (called no-effect values or safe threshold values) are derived for the relevant environmental compartments (water, sediments soil and sewage treatment plants). Copper releases were quantified for the copper industry production and its down-stream uses. Copper levels in the receiving environments were compared against environmental no-effect values for the risk characterization.

The main results and conclusions, summarized in [4] have been refined and finally agreed by TCNES and SCHER [5]. The main conclusions can be summarized as: 

- **Environmental copper releases during production and use are well known.** 

The detaile

d analysis of the emission sources [5] (excluding uses of copper compounds as plant protection products and biocidal products) demonstrate that major copper emissions are related to diffuse emissions from copper compounds used as feed additives and soil fertilizers (39 % of the total EU emissions) and from copper powders used in automobile brake pads (31 % of the total copper EU emission). Only a few “massive” copper markets have measurable emissions during professional/consumer use. Among these, wear of overhead wires, corrosion of copper tubes, fittings and taps and external building applications (roofs, gutters, down pipes, facades) contribute respectively to 9, 5 and 1 % of the total anthropogenic EU emissions. Interestingly, the relative contribution from waste incineration plants and landfill facilities is minor (0.4 %). Other minor copper releases, that have been considered include, among others, industry releases, domestic and industrial heating, fireworks and domestic wastewaters (excl. corrosion). 

- **Copper background values are variable and critical to the understanding of the copper levels in receiving environments.** 

In accordance to the EU Technical Guidance [1], copper concentrations in the receiving environments were estimated from integrating the copper release data into the EU exposure model (EUSES) as well as from monitoring data. #### 4 Important EU regulatory framework applicable to the RA 

The copper RA directly applies to a range of European policies and regulations such as: REACH, Water Framework Directive, Soil protection, Drinking water directive, Products in contact with food, Integrated Pollution Prevention and Control and Sustainable Construction products…. 

The integration of the risk assessment data into these regulations is ongoing as discussed for some of these below: 

##### 4.1 REACH: 

##### Burden of proof on chemical safety from regulators to industry 

The European Council concluded in 2000 that there was a need to reform the European chemicals policy to make it more effective. This has led to the development of a revised EU chemicals management policy, REACH – the Registration, Evaluation and Authorisation of Chemicals. A cornerstone of this policy is that the burden of proof for the safe manufacture and EU market falls onto industry. Importers and manufacturers of substances are obliged to register the substance put on the EU market in >1000 tons by 2010. Failure to register means no market. Registration requires the submission of a technical dossier containing classification proposals, a chemical safety report of risk assessment of all life stages of the substance and, where risks are identified, the risk management measures are put in place to ensure the substance can be produced and used safely. Regulators will evaluate whether the required information has been collected and whether or not the chemical safety report is acceptable. Market restrictions will be imposed when safe use cannot be proven. Substances of very high concern, that is substances which are carcinogenic, mutagenic, have reproductive effects (CMR) or persistent, bioaccumulative and toxic substances (PBT), will only be allowed through an authorisation procedure. 

For metals, the methodologies developed under the risk assessments [6] are to a large extent consistent with those set by REACH. 

For copper, there is no need for the authorization procedure because the RA demonstrated that both CMR and PBT criteria do not apply to copper or copper compounds. 

The copper voluntary risk assessment, posted on the EC REACH website [5], forms the basis for the copper REACH registration of the copper consortium. The copper consortium will also register copper interme

diates, produced during copper production as well final copper slags (full registration).

Subsequent comparison of these quality criteria with national monitoring data has resulted in different levels of compliance in different Member States and therefore has lead to different environmental risk perceptions and environmental policies. These differing environmental policies of EU Member States can result in market distortion through the introduction of inappropriate restrictions on the use of copper products, particularly in the Building Construction sector. Within the European environmental action plan, the harmonization of quality criteria, the criterion for identifying priority substances, and the monitoring and control of priority substances, is a high priority.

#### Abstract 

For a long time, copper smelters have been aware of the duality of the copper slag their usual process generates - a burden and a valuable by-product at the same time! A burden when considered as an expensive waste material to be ponded to fulfil more and more stringent environmental legislations. A valuable by-product when considering the remaining fractions of metals contained within it. If efficiently treated, this slag can provide a value which can offset treatment cost and ideally generate profit. 

Paul Wurth has worked for several years on residue recycling and reuse, and especially on zero waste processes, to recover iron, zinc, copper and other metals such as nickel, silver from metallurgical by-products, using - for example - PRIMUS<sup>®</sup> and i-Meltor™ processes. 

Regarding copper slag, laboratory and piloting tests have demonstrated that, compared with existing slag cleaning technologies, an adapted i-Meltor™ process can improve greatly the recovery of copper through a better yield and a higher value of the output, and under certain conditions increase the overall smelter throughput. 

Indeed, the i-Meltor™ Electric Arc Furnace being very flexible in terms of metallurgical tasks and material input, enables to realise different metallurgical steps for, on the one hand, recovering copper and eventually other precious elements, and on the other hand bleeding-off, in a controlled way, “nasty” impurities – thus favouring the re-use of the final slag. 

Solving an environmental issue and contributing to increased raw material sources through a profit generating metallurgical processes is no longer a dream.

#### 2 PAUL WURTH solutions for processing residues

### Corporate Sustainability

#### Abstract 

Sustainability is understood as a future-compatible and lasting development that meets the requirements of today’s generation, does not compromise the possibilities of future generations and satisfies their needs. Sustainability can be achieved by the integration of different dimensions of social development, which is based on the three pillar model of ecology, economy and social aspects. The ecological and economic dimensions are pursued vigorously at Aurubis and have advanced the production capacity and the company’s options for development and future action. 

Numerous measures have however also been implemented in the social dimension that are aimed at reducing any socially undesirable effects that the company might have and at furthering its positive social impact. These are intended to help make the company a better corporate citizen. For example, the company’s inhouse health management shows how preventive measures for health promotion and occupational safety contribute to improving health. The integrative processing of the social, ecological and economic dimensions is an integral part of corporate policy and should ensure that the company remains a going concern by sustainable management. 

#### 1 Introduction 

The term sustainability is ever-present – in industry, politics, science and technology and in environmental research. It connects questions such as „How do we want to live today or in future?“, „How do we fulfil our obligations – in the company and in the region?“ or „Where do we want to stand in future“. 

These questions are closely connected with the idea of sustainable development,

which has taken on ever increasing significance in corporate activities and focused more strongly on mankind in recent years. Apart from commercial enterprises, governments and NGOs also use this term – each with its own targets and different weighting. 

Since sustainability plays a role in a variety of connections, the associations and understanding of it are inaccurate, ambiguous and also contradict each other. Opinions and statements on sustainability 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

387 

_Hannemann, Lьbbe_ 



therefore differ and discussions are frequently disputed. This hardly satisfactory circumstance is caused by the lack of a set definition that makes the term selective. It should be realistically accepted that sustainability is rather more a process than a circumstance (this comes at the end of sustainable development). While the first clear global targets for sustainability are already apparent, a patent recipe for successfully achieving these goals long-term still does not exist. 

#### 2 Sustainable development from its beginnings until today 

##### 2.1 Beginning of the discussion on sustainability 

The term „sustainability“ was first defined in 1713 in a treatise by the Saxon mining administrator Carl von Carlowitz with “instructions for the natural growing of wild trees“ [1]. He demanded sustainable forestry management, based on the principle that only as much wood should be cut as can grow again. This principle combined both ecological (maintaining the forest as a natural habitat) and economic aspects (maintaining the forest’s maximum production power to ensure its existence) and can also be explained by the economically advantageous logic that a person should live from the “interest” of his capital (the cut wood) and not attack the capital (forest). This principle was later even made law in German forest management. The sustainability term with a concept was not applied to fisheries until the beginning of the 20<sup>th</sup> century, with the aim of creating conditions that would enable a maximum catch depending on the fish populations. The sustainability idea did not succeed in penetrating the other commercial sectors. 

The nature factor was investigated scientifically as of the middle of the eighteenth century. Ideas that nature had a limited load capacity came into focus. Given the exploding population, a disparity between resource quantities in a lebensraum and population numbers was diagnosed, the consequence of which were famine and epidemics. However, hardly any attention was paid at the time to this theory, which has been recognised and proven nowadays, since environmental problems were not topics for political or social debates. This thesis received little resonance until way into the twentieth century and was regarded as refuted since progressive methods in agriculture had improved the food supply and the population was not growing to the same extent as the consumption possibilities. 

This did not change until co

ncerns arose about the more apparent destruction of natural habitats by increasing industrialisation and the spread of urban lifestyles to rural areas. The destruction of nature was however not seen at this time as a problem threatening the existence of mankind, but rather as a selective problem which should be selectively addressed. 

Not until 1970 did ecology movements form, which expressed a changed environmental awareness. The report „Limits to Growth“, published in 1972 on behalf of the Club of Rome, created a contextual bridge to the forestry management term of sustainability that started a scientific and political discussion on the connections of social production styles and lifestyles, economic growth and the finite nature of resources [2]. As a result, the United Nations concerned itself at an 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

388 

_Corporate Sustainability_ 



environmental conference with the subject of sustainability for the first time in 1972 at the initiative of Scandinavian countries. Political declarations on the environment clearly stated in the discussions that the industrialised nations mainly used ecological improvements for themselves, while the poorer countries in the south demanded social and economic development. 

##### 2.2 Brundtlandt Report as the definition of sustainable development 

The World Commission on Environment and Development convened by the United Nations in 1983 published the best-known and politically most important definition of sustainable development. Known by the name of its chairman as the Brundlandt Commission, the commission defined a development as sustainable „if it meets the needs of the present, without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs“ [3]. This approach became the new leitmotif of the international environmental policy [4]. The Brundlandt Report dealt intensively with questions of social justice and distribution, if nothing else to take the interests of the developing countries into account. These countries feared that increasing environmental requirements could represent an additional impairment for their economies and provide them with further disadvantages. 

#### 3 Concept of sustainability 

As the historical development shows, sustainability can only be achieved by the integration of different dimensions of social development. The so-called three pillar model of sustainability has prevailed in theory, which attributes equal significance to the ecology (environment), the economy (wealth) and social aspects (quality of life). The central aim of sustainability is to avoid irreversible damage in all three dimensions. These are dependent on each other and cannot be partially optimised without putting the development process as a whole into question [5, 6]. 

In practice, it has been seen that one of the three pillars are often handled to the detriment of the other pillars, which results in substitution among themselves, but finally the overall benefit

or the charity level remains. Thus, environmental associations are primarily promoted that predominantly treat ecological sustainability, which is considered the prerequisite for appropriate living conditions, ahead of economic and social aspects. This concept is criticised if this weak sustainability is applied for the complete substitutability of natural resources or the belief in technical progress.

#### 4 Sustainability and commercial enterprises 

Corporate activities as regards sustainability can be carried out in a variety of forms and on very different levels. Based on the three pillar model, the following four sustainability challenges result for commercial enterprises [7]: 

- _Ecological challenge:_ Increase in absolute environmental compatibility by reducing the environmental burdens arising. Examples at Aurubis: handling resources economically; avoiding environmental burdens by reducing emissions and waste. 

- _Economic challenge:_ Cost-effective implementation of measures for environmental protection and social commitment increasing profitability and corporate value. Examples: setting up of material flow management; utilisation of environmentally compatible and innovative technologies; projects focused on young people and the immediate neighbourhood (good corporate citizen). 

- _Social challenge:_ Minimising socially undesirable effects which a company causes. Examples: health promotion; local and cultural diversity that promote the paths to sustainable development. 

- _Integration challenges:_ Combination of the three challenges and integration of environmental and social management in the company’s conventional management. 

It can only be decided with hindsight whether a company is sustainable or not. There can be more or less factors contributing to this, with the options of technological and organisational activities. The already established packages relating to individual topics (such as CO2 reduction) are frequently taken as the solution.

#### 5 Stakeholders as interested and affected parties 

Sustainability is an ambitious concept. The aim of reconciling all three challenges requires that the needs are measured. To do this, a dialogue between the stakeholders must be held, which clarifies and weighs up the mutual demands. Sustainable development is therefore a communication task. This is conducted with stakeholders who have an interest in the company’s activities and are inside and outside the company [8]. This relates for example to employees and customers, but also neighbours, environmental associations and the authorities. Companies therefore stay in contact with their stakeholders with the aim of successfully implementing sustainable development. The company’s perspectives improve when cooperative partners get together who use synerg

ies to create something new and stakeholders can be used as a de-escalating factor [9]. 

Aurubis has compiled a sustainability report in accordance with GRI standards (Global Reporting Initiative) for internal and external stakeholders [10], in which Aurubis’s activities and performance in relation to sustainable development are detailed. This sustainability report is standardised and enables comparisons to be made. The analysis of the ecological and social effects of company activities is decisive and enables identified adverse impacts to be reduced. 

Each stakeholder group has expectations, which unites it as regards interests. Thus, for example, employees hope to maintain their quality of life, which can be influenced by working conditions, workplace safety and involvement. 

#### 6 Progress in sustainable development 

Companies in industry mostly dominate the economic and ecological dimension of sustainability. The optimisation of these two aspects enables the sustainable development to be quickly and visibly influenced in a comparably simple way. This is attributable to already available corporate structures such as controlling, maintenance or development, for which new goals must be formulated and which can start their work immediately. The situation with the social dimension looks different. This did not penetrate the companies’ awareness until relatively recently and with varied approaches takes various aspects of sustainability into consideration to different degrees. Special significance here is attributed to Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR), since the European Union promotes it as a contribution to sustainability. The EU defines this term with a concept which serves the companies as a basis in order to voluntarily include social values and environmental requirements in their corporate activities and to integrate the interaction with their stakeholders [11]. Internal commitments are for example human resource management, a social corporate structure and occupational safety; the responsibility for the surroundings and global environmental protection can be named as external commitments. 

Historic development shows that sustainable development is increased connected with the perspectives of CSR on the basis of economic and ecological aspects and therefore confirms the

##### 7.1 Reduction of blood lead levels 

Besides copper, l

ead is also extracted in large quantities at the Hamburg site. About 18,000 tonnes of lead was produced in the last fiscal year. As an element in copper concentrates and various secondary raw materials, it is separated in the various production processes and is finally transferred as lead bullion to the lead refining facility where it is relieved of impurities in several successive refining stages and becomes fine lead as the end product. The refining processes are performed in large-scale melting pots with an open surface. Agitators ensure that there is movement in the pots, while pumps channel the molten lead from one pot to the other. Part of the boiler facility is connected to an off-gas filter plant. 

Metallic lead is only toxic for humans to a certain extent. It forms a thick, insoluble airborne protective layer. By contrast, lead dust and inorganic lead compounds are hazardous, which can be absorbed in the body by breathing or swallowing. Small amounts that can be less than workplace limit values, but absorbed over a longish period, are enriched in the skeleton system, since the lead has a chemical interaction with calcium. A chronic illness manifests itself in weariness, as well as defects in the nervous system and the musculature. The body only eliminates the lead slowly; the biological half-life is 15 years. A lead accumulation in the body can therefore only be reversed to a limited extent. Consequently, priority is being given to forward-looking thoughts on how to avoid the problem. 

Lead can be ingested during production at Aurubis AG by breathing in flue dust. The dust particles necessary are absorbed in the lungs. Working areas where hot melts are processed represent a particularly dangerous source of exposure. Lead intake can also be enteral via the gastrointestinal tract. Insufficient hygiene – particularly in the breaks – can be a cause of this. 

Since the damage potential of lead must be classified as high due to its accumulation, a number of preventive measures were introduced as part of the company health protection, which have contributed to significantly reducing blood lead levels. The otherwise usual hierarchy for measures was eliminated so as to lose as little time as possible. #### Abstract 

The aim of this study is to recovery copper powder from wastewater containing copper in the different field of metallurgy such as, etching solutions and galvanotechnique industries’ waste solutions. To optimize the experimental conditions a synthetic solutions (0.5-10 g L<sup>-1</sup> Cu<sup>2+</sup> and 7.5-15 g L<sup>-1</sup> H2SO4), which simulated the wastewater, was prepared. All experiments were carried out in a rotating cylinder electrode (RCE)-type electrolysis cell with forced convection. In the recovery of copper in powder form, the effect of working conditions such as current density, copper ion concentration and temperature of electrolyte on the morphologies of copper powders were a

nalyzed using the scanning electron microscopy (SEM) technique. Also, their effects on the system data, including current efficiency and specific energy consumption were evaluated. It was found that the shape and structure of electrolytic copper powder particles depend on the electrolysis parameters. #### 1 Introduction 

The amount of heavy metals such as copper, zinc, chromium, etc., is high in industrial wastewater. These metals endanger public health and the environment if discharged without adequate treatment. On the other hand, the heavy metals are very expensive and useful resources, thus, they should be recovered. Metal removal or recovery from wastewater is becoming an increasingly important issue because of growing economic and environmental concerns. 

Copper, the metal considered in this study, is a widely used metal in different industrial areas due to its properties of electric conductivity, ductibility and thermal conductibility. More than 50 % of this metal is used in the electronic industries and about 30–40 % of the copper world production is used for alloy production [1]. During recent years, copper powders have been produced commercially for

Various industrial methods have been developed or investigated for the removal and recovery of metals from wastewater. It is less electropositive than hydrogen and therefore, it can be deposited on cathode before hydrogen reduction. Also, it may be possible to recover the copper in the form of valuable powder and recycle the residual electrolyte by the method of electrolysis. 

The use of electrolytic processes for the recovery of copper in the form of powder or compact cathode product from wastewater has been investigated by a number of researches. Classical electrolysis operations are conducted at relatively high metal ion concentrations and at current values that approximately correspond to 30-35 % of the limiting current density to avoid possible side reactions (reaction 3), to sustain a high current efficiency, and to obtain smooth and compact cathode surfaces. 

In galvanostatic systems, electrodeposit of copper has the tendency to form powders when current density larger than the limiting diffusion current density is used (or overpotentials outside the plateau of the limiting diffusion current density in potentiostatic systems). 

Taking into account this condition, the metal powder recovery from dilute solutions such as wastewater in electrolysis system is possible with specifically arranged electrolysis cells. There are two ways in design of these cells: 

- Increasing the electrode surface (thus, higher current could be applied without increasing the current density and eventually large amounts of materials would be deposited per unit time) 

- Increasing the relative motion between electrode and electrolyte, i.e. increasing the convection (thus, as small as possible diffusion layer thickness can only be obtained) 

In the present work, the RCE-type electrolysis cell, which combines these two types, was used.

#### 3 Experimental 

The experiments were performed in two different types of electrolysis cell (type-A and type-B). Both of them were separated into two sections, anodic and cathodic units, by diaphragm. In the first section, electrolysis is carried out and the second section is the filtration part for preventing metal powders produced from clogging solution circulation pumps. O

ne of the most important technological problems faced in the electrolysis is the continuity of process due to the change in the cathode size. In the designed cells, the metal powder produced is removed from the cathode surface by a scraper which is added back to the solution and then filtered. Thus, cathode size is kept constant and the continuity problem is solved. It is important to note that the cathode-scraper was positioned at a distance of 1 mm from the surface of the cathode. Stainless steel rotating cylinder cathodes with the dimensions of 2 (φ) x 5 ( _h_ ) cm (type-A) and 6 (φ) x 10 ( _h_ ) cm (type-B) were used at laboratory scale electrolysis cells. The cylindrical anode made of lead, which situated around the cathode. 

Total electrolyte volume of type-A was 1.25 L while type-B was filled with 3 L of electrolyte. To optimize the experimental conditions synthetic solutions were prepared. The initial concentrations of these solutions were given below; 

10 g L<sup>-1</sup> Cu<sup>2+</sup> and 15 g L<sup>-1</sup> H2SO4 ( _solution I_ ) 

2 g L<sup>-1</sup> Cu<sup>2+</sup> and 7.5 g L<sup>-1</sup> H2SO4 ( _solution II_ )

### Environmental Improvement of Anode Production at Aurubis in Hamburg 

Frank Hoffmeister, Torben Edens, Matthias Krystkowiak 

Aurubis AG HovestraЯe 50 D-20539 Hamburg, Germany 

**Keywords:** Environmental improvement, exhaust gas system, SO2 treatment 

#### Abstract 

Aurubis is the biggest producer of copper in Europe and the biggest recycler of copper in the world. In total the group has a good 4700 employees. Its core business is the production of copper from copper concentrates, copper scrap and recycled materials followed by the further processing of the copper into rod, continuous cast shapes, rolling products and copper alloys. A major focus of the group's business activities at the Hamburg site is the production of copper in the primary smelter. 

Compared with its international peers, Aurubis is a leader in environmental protection. Through substantial investments in environmental protection and continuous improvement of the production facilities it has been possible for example to reduce emissions apr. 90 % since 1990. 

Aurubis uses efficient, new process technologies and innovative environmental protection methods. The group's high standard of environmental protection is reflected for example in the productionspecific SO2 emissions. The emissions at Hamburg side is 4 kg SO2/tonne copper, compared to 352 kg SO2/tonne copper as average for international smelters [1]. 

In order to achieve the same high environmental standards in the anode production area, a new exhaust gas system was installed there. 

#### 1 The starting point 

##### 1.1 Description of the existing plant 

Approximately 1.2 million tons per year of copper concentrate are processed in the smelter at the Hamburg site. The concentrates are smelted in a flash smelting furnace. The resulting matte is cleaned by means of pyrometallurgical in two Peirce-Smith converters, a process which removes iron as slag and sulphur as sulphur dioxide. Other base metals are slagged or volatilised during the

The newly installed filter system for exhaust gases from anode furnaces and hoods is fully closed from penthouse to first floor. An efficient technology must be used to collect the emissions with the suction system. The investment and operating costs of a suction system increase greatly with the exhausted flow. Therefore it is important to keep the extracted flow as small as possible. The following planning steps were carried out for this purpose:

The most efficient collection off emissions are baffle- or nozzle plate hoods outmatch other common hoods (Figure 6, Case 1). Emission collection essentially depends on the suction velocity at the collection point. The velocity is highest in front of the pipe socket. In the case of a funnel hood (Figure 6, Case 3), the suction socket is far from the emission source (distance A). With this hood, only approx. 22 % of the coverage of a nozzle plate can be achieved. If the pipe is moved closer to the emission source (distance B) the coverage increases to 55 % of a nozzle plate (Figure 6, Case 2). In the case of a nozzle plate (Figure 6, Case 1), the emissions cannot pass the extractor unimpeded. Furthermore, the suction power is directed downwards. The nozzle plate represents the most efficient arrangement for the collection of emissions [3].

#### Abstract 

In the following paper we present the _in situ_ manufacturing technology of nano-powders by electrochemical methods. The potential environment and raw material is the wastewater which is a byproduct of the copper ore flotation process and by-products of the copper electrorefining process. The accumulation of waste is growing engineering and potentially ecological problems. Chemical analysis of the waste showed that a series of metals such as: Cd, Hg, Pb, Cu, Ag, Co, Ni, Hf, Nb, Os, Re, Rh, Sc, Th, V, W, Zn, Zr etc. are contained in solid and liquid fraction. Due to the complex matrix of the wastewater and relatively low concentrations of the metals currently there are no economically viable technologies available to recycle the metals into the market products. The development of nanotechnologies and its commercial applications create the opportunity to exploit the copper wastewater to undertake a manufacturing of nano-powders which are currently commercially used. 

In the present paper we refer the studies concerning development of nano-powders manufacturing technologies based on potential pulse electrolysis from aqueous solution which enable commercial manufacturing of copper and silver nano-powders of chemical purity up to 99.999 %. We also present a novel approach to control size and shape of deposited copper particles and nano-particles from industrial electrolytes. The SEM, EDS and electrochemical measurements results showed tha

The rate of the metals recovery from diluted electrolytes can be easily increased by the increase of mass transport rate. In practice it can be achieved by mixing electrolyte, rotation/movement of electrode and by the application of ultramicro-electrodes (UME) and arrays of ultramicro-electrodes [1, 2]. In the present work we decided to use UME to increase the rate of the mass transfer and consequently the rate of the metals deposition. The mass transfer to UME is increased due to spherical diffusion of electrolyte to the surface of the electrode [3-5]. The pilot installation capable of manufacturing of approximately 10 kg of nano-powders per day consists of the following basic elements: 

- industrial electrolyte container, approx. 1500 l 

- copper concentration sensor 

- electrolyser 300-500 l 

- moving cathode – stainless steel (immersed from 0.2 to 0.4 s in the solution) 

- anode: either Cu or Dimensionally Stable Anode (DSA) 

- filtration system, rinsing by water or/and non-aqueous solvent 

- rectifier, 1000 A 

- drying and packaging of product in inert atmosphere (e.g. nitrogen gas) 

The technology to manufacture copper and silver nano-particles and particles from concentrated industrial electrolytes can be realised either to manufacture e.g. copper nano-particles and in this case a soluble copper anode (grade A) is used. When additionally purifying of the electrolyte occurs DSA anode is used instead of soluble (copper). 

#### 3 Conclusions 

The technology based on the usage of ultramicro-electrodes and potentiostatic electrolysis is an important development to purify/recover effectively metals from low concentration, complex matrix waste waters and by-products. Potentiostatic electrolysis enables obtaining very high purity cathodic copper and silver (and other metals) from diluted solutions. The economic viability of the process is assured by the application of ultramicro-electrodes and ultramicro-electrodes arrays at which spherical (non-linear) diffusion occurs leading to very high cathodic current densities reaching a few amperes per cm<sup>2</sup> . The products of the process are high added value nano- and micro-particles of copper and silver which can be sold at prices from $1000 to $2000 per kg. The size and shape of the metals nano-particles can be controlled by the proper choice of metal base and potential and time of electrodeposition. 

Finally, on the basis of the obtained results (high purity of deposited copper from industrial electrolytes) potentiostatic electrolysis with convective diffusion conditions at flat electrodes (not

Patricio Pйrez O., J. Joaquнn Jara D.

#### Abstract 

A high labour productivity is an essential element for companies in order to compete in the mining industry. However, the factors that influence its behaviour have not been extensively studied. In this paper we use a panel data approach to identify and analyze the variables behind the changes in mining workforce output in the copper industry. 

The paper comprises five countries that together represent over 60 % of world total copper production and are a reference for the industry. The results of the analysis show that better deposits and operational factors are not enough to explain labour productivity improvements in the copper mining industry, and instead, company specific efforts, country and industry changes are as important as the reserve base and geological characteristics of the operation. 

#### 1 Introduction 

Labour productivity is an essential driver for companies in order to compete in the mining industry. However, the factors that influence its behaviour have not been extensively studied. In the last 20 years there have been some stu

dy cases that has analyzed the evolution of this variable for the copper mining industry in different countries. In Tilton and Landsberg [1], the collapse and subsequent recovery of the US industry between 1970 and 1995 was reviewed. In this work, they conclude that jumps in productivity due to the development of new technologies and other innovations were essential to overcome the drop of competitiveness caused by the deterioration of mining conditions. In this process, the introduction of SX-EW technology played a central role. In other article, Aydin and Tilton [2] analyzed the effects of new production (new deposits get into production) and the introduction of new technologies and innovations on productivity changes. They note that, in the case of US industry in the period 1975-1995, the impact of new production on labour productivity was marginal. In the other hand, innovation, development and diffusion of technology were essen-

tial for meaningful and sustainable improvements over time. These findings have relevant consequences. First, is likely that geographical patterns of mining activities could change in the future. Second, companies and countries that wish to maintain or increase its mining competitive position must necessarily emphasize not only their natural endowment, but also other elements like a positive investment climate and a friendly environment for innovation. And third, positive trend in productivity growth, and the consequent fall in costs, could be perpetuated by an innovative culture and a favourable disposition to new technologies inside the organizations. 

In the other hand, Tilton [3] examined the relationship between labour productivity, costs and the survival of mines during a recession period. It concludes that the level of productivity at the start of the downturn is less relevant to survive than the mine’s ability to increase its productivity and lower its costs during the recession. Also, the work notes that those mines with higher reserves have stronger incentives to invest in improvements and increase productivity than those mines with less endowments and a shorter life. 

In the case of the Chilean copper industry, Garcia et al. [4] studied the source of productivity growth between 1978 and 1997. The authors found that over 50 % of the raise in production during the period came from new operations, affecting the productivity trend. They conclude that, unlike the US situation during the previous decades, in the case of Chile the new production was responsible for a big part of the increase in labour productivity, although the contribution of innovation and technological change were relevant too.

Now, one of the main advantages of panel data techniques is that the inclusion of temporal dimension enriches the nature of the data and the control of the variables, even when they are unobserved. To do this, we assume that the error in the model is given by the following expression: µit = δi + εit where δi is a specific effect for each operation and reflects this unobserved heterogeneity, and εit is a white noise or natural variability of the process. To obtain within estimators consistent with data length N and width T, both Qit and Zit must be assumed strictly exogenou

However, in mining industries companies generally do not determine the output level that allows profit maximization, instead they usually produce at maximum capacity. In this case, since the amount of data for most groups is relatively large, and according to the large numbers theory, the parameters would be consistent or the bias would be fairly minor, not affecting the quality of the results. 

The time effect τt captures the variation at group level in period t. Such variations could arise from changes in regulations which is common throughout the industry, changes in copper prices, costs and other inputs, etc. Although, this changes must affects the industry as a whole to be incorporated by this effect.

###### 3.3.1 Fixed Effects 

The fixed effect αi represents the base level of productivity of each mine, so that the FEt index shows its evolution and how the level for each subgroup is changing over time. If available technology for copper mining was stable through the years, and the most productive operations were exploited first, the FEt index would tend to decline in the course of time. On the other hand, if the technology introduced through new capital increases permanently, then the FEt index would tend to increase. Finally, if there were a balance between keeping the least productive mines in operation and the incorporation of new technology, so that two opposite forces were cancel, this index would remain stable and would not observe large jumps over the period analysis. However, San Manuel production decreased by 53 % in 1999 (from 103 to 48 thousand MT), and thus their relative importance. #### 4 Concluding remarks 

The evolution of labour productivity in the minerals and mining industry has been analyzed by some case studies. The evidence indicates that the adoption of new technologies and new production (new mines) with better exploitation conditions could explain a big portion of the changes in 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

462

this sector. Nevertheless, the specific factors behind labour productivity evolution are not completely understood. 

This paper analyzes the forces that have been leading the changes in labour productivity in the copper mining industry in the period 1992 to 2009, and making a comparison between the most important producer countries, with particular reference to Chile. Using panel data analysis for 7 countries (Australia, Canada, Chile, Peru, Russia-Kazakhstan, United States and Zambia-DR Congo) and a methodology to decompose the changes in productivity, the research has found some relevant issues. 

First, we find that productivity patterns differ according to the process at each mine type, i.e. if they are underground or open pit. This leads to perform a separate analysis for both types of production. 

The results show that production levels and head grades have a positive effect in productivity, while in open pit mines the stripping ratios has a negative one. The above results are in line with that reported in previous studies and with the economic intuition. In the other hand, the effect of reserves on labour productivity is not completely clear. A possible explanation for this result could arise by the strong relationship between the reserves revaluation process and the copper prices. Finally, the data also show that the various countries in the sample are affected differently by each of the variables considered in the study. 

Indeed, in the case of underground mining, in Australia the movement of labour productivity has been influenced mainly by cross country changes, collected by the residual time component of the regression. In the case of Peru, the scale effect is predominant, while in the US productivity trends are a reflection of all variables interaction. Regarding the evolution of open pit mining, Peru's behaviour is remarkable: the price effect determines the evolution of productivity mainly between 1993 and 1998, after which this effect remains high but stable. For Australia, the increase in labour productivity in the first half of the analysis period reflects the impact of the residual effect and the scale effect, which offset the decline in the fixed effects. Starting in 2002, the residual time effect is the one who leads the downward trend in productivity in that country. 

One of the contributions of this work is to analyze explicitly the relationship between

the geological factors and the productivity of each mine. This allows a more accurate approximation of the elements behind labour productivity, rather than attributing them to the fixed effects. It is striking that geological factors show a rather small contribution in explaining its evolution. 

In the case of Chile, it could be concluded that the increase of SX-EW operations, with better operational conditions, played a relevant role in the jump in productivity observed in the open pit mines in the early 90’s. In the case of underground production, have been a variety of factors that explain the evolution of labour productivity. The initial increase period extending from 1992 to 1997 could be mainly explained by the central role of Codelco, introducing technologies and systematic and successive improvements in management. Then, between 1997 and 2002, the price effect becomes important. The observed decline in copper prices during those years puts pressure on the companies, who were forced to make improvements to remain competitive and stay on the market.

#### Abstract 

The National Mining Company (ENAMI), on its project for increasing the treatment capacity of liquid effluents from its acid plant of the Paipote Smelter, developed a research Project with Universidad de Concepciуn, to determine the feasibility of producing gypsum as an intermediate product during the liquid effluent neutralization process. A pilot plant with two agitated reactors in series, with 100 litres of capacity each were built, and allowed to simulate and evaluate a continuous neutralization process. The effluents contain approximately 75 g/l sulphuric acid and impurities coming from the gas scrubbing stage, before they enter the acid plant. Results indicate that it is, in fact, feasible to obtain clean gypsum when neutralizing the liquid effluents with lime when the neutralization pH is equal or less than 1. An aspect that must be considered when implementing this alternative is to characterize the presence of solids in suspension that could be contained on the acid effluent.

### Production of Elemental Sulphur from SO2 

M. Rameshni, S. Santo WorleyParsons 125 West Huntington Drive Arcadia, California 91007, USA 

**Keywords:** Production, sulphur, emissions, SO2, reduction, operational stability 

#### Abstract 

WorleyParsons innovative SO2 reduction process efficiently recovers sulphur from SO2 streams. Effluent gases from ore roasters and smelters and coal-fired power plants can be treated to reduce sulphur emissions. This exciting new process is an innovative combination of well-established processes of reaction of CH4 and sulphur vapour to produce CS2, followed by catalytic hydrolysis of CS2 to H2S, and Claus reaction of H2S and SO2 to sulphur. Key advantages are lower fuel consumption, reduced emissions, better product sulphur quality and better operational stability. 

#### 1 Introduction 

Environmental regulatory agencies of many countries continue to promulgate more stringent standards for sulphur emissions from Industrial sources. Many plants around the world, smelters in particular, are still allowed to emit large quantities of SO2 because of their remote locations and the high cost of mitigation, but those exemptions are running out as governments become more environmentally responsible. With the renewed interest in high sulphur coal for power production and increased activity in the mining and metals sectors, it is necessary to develop and implement reliable and cost-effective technologies to cope with the changing requirements. 

Sulphur dioxide is found in a many industrial gases emanating from plants involved in roasting, smelting and sintering sulphide ores, or gases from power plants burning high sulphur coal or fuel oils or other sulphurous ores or other industrial operations involved in the combustion of sulphurbearing fuels, such as fuel oil. One of the more difficult environmental problems facing industry is how to economically control SO2 emissions from these sources. 

In general, smelter gases contain about 2 % to 16 % SO2 by volume while gases from other sources may vary from 1 % to 100 % SO2 with the other components usually comprising oxygen, nitrogen, carbon dioxide and water vapour. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

477 

_Rameshni, Santo_ 



Few commercially feasible processes for the reduction of SO2 to elemental sulphur have been developed. The reduction of SO2 to elemental sulphur has been investigated extensively over a period of nearly 100 years, and the basic SO2 reduction process using a hydrocarbon reducing agent is discussed in many articles and patents. Thermal and catalytic reduction

processes have both been investigated over the years. 

The general problems using hydrocarbon as a reducing agent are listed below. 

- Low sulphur recovery efficiency 

- High fuel consumption 

- High cost 

- Difficult operation 

- Soot formation produces off-colour sulphur and fouls catalyst beds 

- By products, such as hydrogen and CO, increase the gas volume requiring larger plants 

With catalytic processes, temperature control is very important because high temperatures can lead to uncontrolled reactions that produce increasing amounts of hydrogen and CO. Therefore, catalytic processes add the following additional problems. 

- Limited ability to control temperature 

- Limited ability to control side reactions 

- Use of staged or switching reactors to control the temperature 

Later work has suggested that the addition of elemental sulphur with the hydrocarbon reducing agent helps to initiate the reduction reactions and reduce soot and byproduct formation. While adding elemental sulphur to the hydrocarbon improves the process, it does not resolve all of the issues. 

Considering all of the problems associated with the current technology, the ore roasting, smelting and clean coal technology leaders are looking for improved technology to convert SO2 to sulphur where potential sulphuric acid supply exceeds demand. A new sulphur recovery technology that offers higher quality sulphur, improved recovery and lower energy consumption is needed. Over the past 50 years, WorleyParsons has actively pursued innovative schemes for the conversion of SO2 to sulphur. 

#### 2 Industrial Practice 

The usual approach has been to directly reduce SO2 to sulphur by thermal or catalytic reaction with a hydrocarbon or carbonaceous fuel as the reducing agent. The hydrocarbon reducing agent can be a gas, liquid or solid. Natural gas, often considered as methane (CH4) for simplicity, is the most commonly employed. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

478 

_Production of Elemental Sulphur From SO2_ 



Development of the technology is seen in the following schemes. These schemes have been confined to laboratory or pilot scale research, conceptual patents or small-scale commercial units. There are several fundamental problems common to these efforts. In particular, byproduct formation of H2S, CS2, COS, H2 and CO reduces sulphur recovery and fuel efficiency and requires larger equipment because of the increased gas flow. Soot formation reduces the quality of the sulphur product and fouls the equipment and catalyst beds reducing the reliability of the unit. 

##### 2.1 Thermal Reduction of SO2 to Sulphur 

During 1909-11, S. W. Young investigated reduction of SO2 with methane and other hydrocarbons on a laboratory scale [1]. Results were disappointing, and no further work was done along these lines for several years. It is assumed that inability to accommodate byproduct H2S, CS2 and COS was considered a key drawback. 

In a 1934 article, Yushkevich, and others, dis

cuss in detail the various possible reaction products from the combination of SO2 and a hydrocarbon reducing agent, including H2S, COS, CS2 and sulphur. Experiments suggested 900-1000 °C as the optimum temperature. [2, 3] 

In 1938, American Smelting and Refining Company (ASARCO) initiated investigations, which soon indicated that relatively low-grade SO2 might be directly converted to reasonably pure sulphur by reduction with natural gas [1]. Laboratory and small-scale pilot operations were gradually expanded until a semi-commercial 5-tpd unit was operated during 1940-45. Gas from copper roasters or converters containing 5-8 % SO2 and 9-12 % oxygen was combusted with sufficient natural gas to consume all the oxygen to CO2. Additional fuel was added to react with an appropriate portion of the SO2 according to the following overall reaction with CH4 as shown in Equation 1. 

2SO2 + CH4 → 2H2O + CO2 + S2 (1) 

Considerable quantities of byproduct H2S, COS and CS2 were formed as well. Furnace temperatures of at least 1250 °C were considered necessary to minimise soot, which would discolour the sulphur. The gases were then cooled and passed through a series of Claus stages for hydrolysis of COS and CS2 to H2S and reaction of residual H2S and SO2 to sulphur according to the Claus reaction. 

This process is still employed today where potential sulphuric acid supply exceeds demand. While the technology has improved, soot formation still tends to reduce sulphur quality and catalyst life. In addition, fuel consumption and emissions are high. 

In 1978, Davy Powergas GmbH proposed a staged combustion process where hydrocarbon gas is burned at near stoichiometric conditions, followed by injection of supplemental CH4 and SO2 which react to form elemental sulphur [4]. It is also claimed that the presence of water vapour in the SO2 feed stream suppresses soot formation. The process was never commercialized. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

479 

_Rameshni, Santo_ 



##### 2.2 Catalytic Reduction of SO2 to Sulphur 

In 1934, United Verde Copper Company proposed a process where a portion of the SO2 stream is combined with CH4 at 800-850 °C in the presence of a metal sulphide catalyst to produce H2S, which is subsequently reacted with the remaining SO2 to yield sulphur according to the Claus reaction [5]. The Claus stage preferably comprised a bed of granular absorbent, such as bauxite or charcoal, continually wetted by a thin film of liquid water which served to absorb the reaction heat and also carry away the product sulphur for subsequent recovery by filtration or sedimentation. The process was never commercialized, but would probably have suffered from the same temperature control and soot formation problems seen in later processes. 

In 1965, Texas Gulf Sulphur patented the reduction of SO2 with hydrocarbons (e.g.: CH4) at 7501000 °C using a catalyst such as alumina, initially achieving 40-60 % sulphur recovery [6]. Two similar catalytic stages typically f

ollowed, whereby the second stage achieved the following at 390 °C. 

- Hydrolysis of byproduct COS and CS2 to H2S 

- Claus reaction of H2S and SO2 to form sulphur 

- Reduction of SO2 by CO and H2 to sulphur 

Claus reaction of residual H2S and SO2 further proceeded in the third stage for 95 % overall sulphur recovery. No method of controlling the heat release from the reduction reactions is described and the process was never commercialized. 

In 1975, Allied Chemical Corp. claimed to have discovered that, at SO2 concentrations of the order of 50 % and higher, a small amount of elemental sulphur (0.1-3 mol-% of the feed gas as S8) lowered the initiation temperature for SO2 reduction and favorably moderated the temperature rise and rate. The sulphur also expedited the reaction and minimised byproduct H2, CO, COS and CS2 formation [3]. Generation of H2 and CO is particularly counterproductive because it decreases sulphur recovery and fuel efficiency and requires larger equipment because of the increased tail gas volume. While the addition of the sulphur does lower the initiation temperature and moderate the temperature rise, the inlet temperature to the reactor is still about 600 °C and the outlet temperature is very high at about 1000 °C. Such high temperatures require the use of expensive reactors and heat exchangers. 

In 1977, Allied Chemical presented an innovative 3-bed arrangement that was claimed to optimise reactant concentrations and temperatures [7]. The total SO2 stream is mixed with a portion of the CH4 and passed through the first reactor to effect reduction of a portion of the SO2 to H2S and sulphur. #### 4 WorleyParsons Innovative SO2 Reduction Process 

WorleyParsons’ innovative (patent pending) SO2 reduction process for sulphur recovery from an SO2 stream is a novel combination of two well-established processes. The scheme includes a CS2 section and a Claus section. 

- **CS2 section** – reaction of natural gas and recycled sulphur vapour to produce CS2 

- **Claus section** – subsequent concurrent catalytic hydrolysis of CS2 to H2S and reaction of H2S and SO2 to produce elemental sulphur in a conventional Claus unit

##### 4.1 SO2 Concentration 

While any SO2 concentration can be processed (following particulate removal), pre-concentrating the raw stream is generally desirable to reduce the Claus tail gas volume, thus [1] reducing the size of the Claus train, [2] increasing recovery, and [3] reducing incinerator fuel. For the SO2 concentration step, there are four well-known processes in the market. 

Outokumpu offers a cold-water based process. The Labsorb (ELSORB) process uses a buffered aqueous solution of sodium salts of phosphoric acid as the solvent. Cansolv uses a chemical solvent based on a proprietary diamine. 

ClausMaster (formerly Solinox) from Monsanto uses a physical solvent (tetra-ethylene-glycol dimethyl-ether). 

A further advantage of such pre-concentration is that the incinerated Claus tail gas can be treated with the solvent to increase sulphur recovery efficiency to nearly 100 %. 

##### 4.2 CS2 Background 

Those of us focused on sulphur recovery tend to view CS2 as an undesirable contaminant rather than a useful feedstock. However, CS2 has been an industrially important chemical for over one hundred years. 

Most of carbon disulphide produced worldwide goes into manufacturing viscose rayon and cellophane film. Carbon disulphide is also used in manufacturing numerous organic sulphur compounds for a variety of applications including rubber vulcanization accelerators, flotation chemicals, pharmaceutical intermediates, fungicides, and insecticides. 

Carbon disulphide, CS2, is a highly volatile, flammable, clear, colorless, dense liquid that has many useful chemical and physical properties. Low concentrations of carbon disulphide naturally discharge into the atmosphere from certain soils, and carbon disulphide has been detected in mustard oil, volcanic gases, and crude petroleum. Carbon disulphide is an unintentional by-product of many combustion and high temperature industrial processes where sulphur compounds are present. 

Carbon disulphide was first prepared nearly two hundred years ago by heating sulphur with charcoal. That general approach was the only commercial route to carbon disulphide until processes for reaction of sulphur and methane or other hy

drocarbons appeared in the 1950s. Significant commercial production of carbon disulphide began around 1880, primarily for agricultural and solvent applications. Both the physical and chemical properties of carbon disulphide are utilized in industry. Commercial uses grew rapidly from about 1929 to 1970, when the principal applications included

##### 4.4 Process Chemistry 

Pure elemental sulphur vapour is catalytically reacted with natural gas to produce hydrogen sulphide (H2S) and carbon disulphide (CS2), according to the following endothermic reactions shown in Equations 4, 5, and 6. 

|CH4+ 2 S2 →CS2+ 2 H2S|(4)|
|---|---|
|2 C2H6+ 7 S2 →4 CS2+ 6 H2S|(5)|
|C3H8+ 5 S2 →3 CS2+ 4 H2S|(6)|



However, the C3+ content of the feed gas should be < 1% to minimise side reactions resulting from cracking. 

At 400-700 °C, reaction 1 equilibrium exceeds 99.9 %. Approximately 5-10 % excess sulphur is typically maintained to minimise byproduct H2, as shown in Equation 7, for example, in the case of methane.

After cooling the stream to condense residual sulphur, the concentrated H2S/CS2 is reheated and combined with the essentially pure sulphur dioxide (SO2) in a fixed catalyst bed, where the H2S and SO2 react to form elemental sulphur according to the Claus reaction shown in Equation 8. 

2 H2S + SO2 → 3 S + 2 H2O (8) 

CS2 is concurrently hydrolyzed to H2S consuming water from Reaction 8 to supply additional H2S according to Equation 9. 

CS2 + 2 H2O → CO2 + 2 H2S (9) 

The reactor effluent is cooled to condense most of the sulphur vapour. Since reactions 8 and 9 are exothermic, the bulk of the ga

s stream is recycled, following reheating, to the reactor to dilute the reactants as necessary to limit the temperature rise. 

The Claus reaction is equilibrium-limited, and the tail gas is ultimately passed through second and third conversion stages to achieve 98 % overall sulphur recovery. 

##### 4.5 CS2 Section Process Description 

The natural gas feedstock and liquid sulphur are separately preheated to 650 °C, at 500 kPag, in an externally fired tubular heater. The heater design is similar to designs commonly used in ethylene cracking. Heat transfer to the tube coil occurs primarily by radiation with no direct contact of the flames. Design is critical to achieve uniform heating to avoid rapid corrosion at hot spots. The tubes are typically constructed of a high nickel-chrome alloy. 

The liquid sulphur vapourizes at around 450°C, at which temperature it exists mainly as S8. Subsequent superheating to 575-650 °C results in endothermic decomposition to smaller, more reactive, species (S6 and S2). This dissociation is also favored by the reduction in partial pressure of the sulphur vapour as H2S and CS2 are formed in the reactor. Consequently, it is desirable to preheat the vapour to the maximum reaction temperature before combination with the natural gas, to minimise the reactor temperature drop resulting from the endothermic dissociation of the sulphur. 

The gas and sulphur vapour are then mixed, typically in a special venturi nozzle. The combined steam flows through a radiantly heated pipe coil, where some reaction takes place, before entering an adiabatic catalytic reactor containing activated alumina catalyst. The gas hourly space velocity is typically 100-400 volumes of gas per hour/unit volume of catalyst. 

As mentioned, 5-10 % excess sulphur is typically fed to maximise natural gas conversion and minimise side reactions. Assuming a fairly constant SO2 rate, it is expected that the sulphur rate would be maintained fairly constant, and the methane automatically adjusted to achieve the optimum ratio of H2S:SO2 = 2:1 at the SRU. 

The effluent gas from the final CS2 reactor is cooled to 340 °C in a waste heat boiler generating high-pressure (4200 kPag) steam, then subsequently to 150 °C by the generation of low-pressure
