### Clean Water for Environment and Production 

Innovative Water Treatment Processes for the Mining Industry 

Dipl.-Ing. Yun Zeng Dr. Richard Woodling Siemens AG Siemens Water Technologies SchuhstraЯe 60 Research and Development Erlangen, Germany Singapore 

**Keywords:** Water, environment, mining industry, innovation 

#### Abstract 

Since years water issues have become one of the major challenges of the mining industry. It is even doubted whether this could be solved at all. Siemens is taking this tough challenge as a responsibility and trying to give the appropriate answer for the industry and also environment. 

In some key mining countries the miners are suffering from water shortage and competition with other fresh water users in the region. Siemens is offering large desalination plants, which are based on membrane technology and have been successfully implemented in other industries. This technology ensures new water resources for sustainable development of the mining industry. 

The beneficiation process generates large quantities of waste water and process water with complex composition. Siemens has developed a special solution, which consists of different state-of-art water treatment processes and is optimized for the mining water properties with high concentration o

f metal ions and sulfate. Treated water can meet the most strictly discharge regulations and can be directly discharged into the nature. This Siemens patented process is till now one of the best possibilities for solving the special water problems in mining industry. 

Based on long term technology know-how of Siemens a break through process for the next generation mining water treatment is still under development. It could bring higher quote of water recovery and lower costs for the operation. 

#### 1 Introduction 

For several years, water issues have been one of the major challenges in the mining industry. On the one hand mines require a large amount of fresh water for the processing. This is mostly supplied by underground water or surface water. In some regions the mining industry is already the biggest water consumer and has become a competitor against other water users. For example, in 2009 Chile's 

577 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

_Zeng, Woodling_ 



state copper commission Cochilco predicted that Region II, the most active mining area in Chile, will consume 57 % of the total water used [1]. Alternative water resource has been discussed in industry since years. Some mining pioneers have decided to use desalinated sea water for the process supply, e.g. Minera Escondida has started one of the biggest desalination project in South America [2]. Siemens has successfully implemented large desalination plants in other industries for years, e.g. in 2006 Siemens has delivered a 35,000 m³/d desalination plant for Yuhuan power plant in China. With the help of modern energy recovery equipment it is thus possible to produce high quality fresh water at acceptable costs. 

On the other hand only less than 1 % of the materials mined constitute the valuable mineral products. Most of the materials mined together with water and the consumed chemicals are disposed as mine wastes in a dam. Until now there has been no data available on the global production of mine wastes [3]. This may result in serious environmental challenges on mid- to long-term. Siemens is working on an intelligent water management system, which address water scarcity and also environmental challenge of mine water disposal. 

To solve this problem calls for innovation. Siemens has served the mining industry for decades and is aware of the particular challenges of the mining industry: harshness of environment, need for highest availability of equipments, high security standards, etc. With regard to water, the challenge lies in reducing consumption, thus increasing efficiency in the use of water, both for the benefit of the environment and for cost-saving. Siemens has filed a patent for a special process for treating the contaminated mine water and making it into high quality water, which could even used for commercial purposes. 

#### 2 Highly Efficient Reuse of Water 

Increasing water usage helps mines save freshwater and at the same time reduces the amount of waste. The Siemens pro

cess is able to treat the tailing dam water or heavily contaminated mine water and makes it into high quality freshwater, which can be reused for the process and even for other commercial usages. It is well known that the mine water is mainly contaminated with inorganic compounds, especially heavy metals and sulfate [4]. State-of-the-art technology uses lime to precipitate metal hydroxide and gypsum. However the dissolved solids residues after lime treatment are still very high, normally 2- constituting several thousand mg/L or even more, e.g. sulfate (SO4 ) after the neutralization by lime can be still at about 2600 mg/L [5]. The presence of high concentrations of dissolved solids impacts in an unexpectedly negative way on flotation. It was confirmed by mine operators that the empirical value for the maximal total dissolved solids (TDS) requested are at 500 mg/L. Another challenge is the discharge of wastewater into a natural environment. In some key mining countries, mining operations are strictly regulated. In Chile, for example, water discharge into the 578 _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ _Clean Water for Environment and Production_ nature environment is subject to standard NCh 1333, which states that the maximum sulfate should be at 250 mg/L [6]. The conventional lime dosing process is not able to reach this limitation. To meet the increasing requirements new innovative processes are required. ##### 2.1 Process Description The core elements of the Siemens process are ion exchange (IX), reverse osmosis (RO), precipitation and clarification in a unique and cost effective manner. Before the influent goes into the core process it is filtrated by a multi-media-filter (MMF) to remove suspended solids. A strong acid cation (SAC) ion exchange resin process then follows which involves exchanging the dissolved ‘Ca2+ ’ for ‘Na+ ’. As Figure 1 shows, sulfate removal is achieved by two-stage reverse osmosis. The RO concentrate, which contains large amounts of Na2SO4, is then mixed with the spent regenerant (CaCl2) to precipitate gypsum. Further reduction of calcium via carbonate precipitation is also utilized. The precipitation effluent is concentrated by a third RO system (SW RO2) to produce a brine solution which is employed for regenerating the SAC IX beds. Tailing

One of the biggest challenges for the process design is the high scaling tendency; especially in the case of tailing water treatment the gypsum precipitation can easily proceed if no pre-treatment is applied. With the ion exchanger an almost calcium free feed is prepared, during the tests the calcium concentration can be controlled at about 20 mg/L for all the RO feeds, this low calcium concentration ensures the concentration product of calcium and sulfate is lower than the solubility, so that the scaling can be avoided. Normally the strong acid ion exchanger needs salt tablets for regeneration. Siemens process takes the RO concentrate as a salt source and after stages of chemical treatment it is able to be used to regenerate the ion exchanger.
